lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure App Service app named App1 that contains two running instances.  
  
You have an autoscale rule configured as shown in the following exhibit.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783645828157-3472y3jb.png)  
  
For the **Instance limits** scale condition setting, you set **Maximum** to **5**.  
  
During a **30-minute** period, App1 uses **80 percent** of the available memory.  
  
What is the maximum number of instances for App1 during the **30-minute** period?
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor autoscale evaluates the configured metric over the specified duration and, when the condition is met, performs the configured scale action. Here, the rule scales out when **Memory Percentage** is **greater than 70%** for **15 minutes**, and each trigger **increases the instance count by 1** with a **5-minute cooldown**. Because the metric dimension is set to **All values**, autoscale evaluates the aggregated metric across the instances rather than requiring each instance to exceed the threshold individually. Starting from **2** instances, sustained **80%** memory can trigger one scale-out after 15 minutes and a second scale-out later in the same 30-minute window, so the highest instance count reached is **4**.

This aligns with Azure Backup requirements for deleting a Recovery Services vault.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains the virtual networks shown in the following table.

All the virtual networks are peered. Each virtual network contains nine virtual machines.  
  
You need to configure secure RDP connections to the virtual machines by using Azure Bastion.  
  
What is the minimum number of Bastion hosts required?
questions.explanation:
Azure Bastion works with both same-region virtual network peering and global virtual network peering across Azure regions. Once a single Bastion host is deployed in any one of the mutually peered virtual networks, it can be used to connect to virtual machines in every peered network, regardless of which region they are in. Since all ten virtual networks in the table are peered together, a single Bastion host is enough to provide RDP access to every VM.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription with Traffic Analytics configured.

- **Region:** East US  
- **Virtual network:** VNet1  
- **NIC network security group:** NSG1  
  
You need to monitor traffic for VM1 by using Traffic Analytics.  
  
Which settings should you configure?
questions.explanation:
Traffic Analytics uses flow log data to analyze network traffic. For a virtual machine associated to a network security group, the required configuration is to enable NSG flow logs on that NSG so Traffic Analytics can process the traffic records. VM diagnostic settings, NSG diagnostic settings, and VM Insights do not supply the Network Watcher flow-log data that Traffic Analytics relies on.

**Learn more:** [Traffic Analytics Overview - Azure Network Watcher](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/traffic-analytics) · [NSG Flow Logs Overview - Azure Network Watcher](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/nsg-flow-logs-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to automate the deployment of a virtual machine scale set that uses the **Windows Server 2016 Datacenter** image.  
  
You need to ensure that when the scale set virtual machines are provisioned, they have web server components installed.  
  
Which **two** actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

Create a new virtual machine scale set in the Azure portal

questions.explanation:
Installing web server components on scale set instances at provision time is a post-deployment configuration task typically handled by a VM Scale Set extension, such as the Custom Script Extension or DSC extension. The installation logic must be provided in a script or configuration file, and the scale set deployment must reference that extension through the `extensionProfile` in the Azure Resource Manager template so each instance runs it when provisioned.

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You plan to create an Azure container registry named ContReg1.  
  
You need to ensure that signed images can be pushed to and pulled from ContReg1.  
  
What should you do for ContReg1?

options.text: Enable encryption by using a customer-managed key.

questions.explanation:
Docker Content Trust enables Azure Container Registry to push signed images and to validate signed images when they are pulled. Encryption with a customer-managed key protects stored data, connected registries support registry synchronization, and tokens provide authentication rather than image-signing capability. Microsoft has deprecated Docker Content Trust and, as of May 31, 2026, it cannot be enabled on newly created registries; however, it is the supplied option that implements signed-image push and pull.

**Learn more:** [Manage signed images by using Docker Content Trust in Azure Container Registry](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-content-trust) · [Transition from Docker Content Trust to Notary Project](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-au/azure/container-registry/container-registry-content-trust-deprecation)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains 20 virtual machines, a network security group (NSG) named NSG1, and two peered virtual networks named VNET1 and VNET2.  
  
You plan to deploy an Azure Bastion Basic SKU host named Bastion1 to VNET1.  
  
You need to configure NSG1 to permit inbound access to the virtual machines through Bastion1.  
  
Which port should you configure for the inbound security rule?
questions.explanation:
Azure Bastion uses HTTPS on port 443 for user access to the Bastion service, but the Bastion host reaches the target virtual machines over their management ports inside the virtual network: TCP 22 for SSH or TCP 3389 for RDP. Microsoft’s Azure Bastion NSG guidance requires allowing inbound traffic from the AzureBastionSubnet to the target VM subnet on ports 22 and 3389. Since 3389 is not an available option here, the correct listed port is 22.

**Learn more:** [Configure NSG rules for Azure Bastion | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bastion/bastion-nsg) · [Azure Bastion | Microsoft Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/azure-bastion/)

questions.question:
Solution: You restart the NetLogon service on a domain controller.  
  
Does this solution meet the goal?
questions.explanation: Restarting the NetLogon service on a domain controller does not trigger synchronization from on-premises Active Directory to Azure AD. In a hybrid identity setup, immediate replication to Azure AD must be initiated from the DirSync/Azure AD Connect server by starting a synchronization cycle, such as a delta sync. Because the requirement is to replicate the newly created user information to Azure AD immediately, restarting NetLogon on a domain controller does not satisfy that requirement.

questions.question:
Solution: You use Active Directory Sites and Services to force replication of the Global Catalog on a domain controller.  
  
Does the solution meet the goal?
questions.explanation: Forcing Global Catalog replication on a domain controller only updates replication within the on-premises Active Directory environment. It does not initiate the synchronization process from the directory synchronization server to Azure AD. To send a newly created on-premises user to Azure AD immediately, the required action is to trigger a directory synchronization cycle on the sync server, such as Azure AD Connect/DirSync.

questions.question:
Solution: You execute the `Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial` PowerShell cmdlet.  
  
Does this solution meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
`Start-ADSyncSyncCycle` starts an Azure AD Connect synchronization cycle on demand. Using `-PolicyType Initial` runs a full synchronization cycle, which includes importing and synchronizing new on-premises Active Directory objects to Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD). Therefore, it does achieve the requirement to replicate a newly created user account immediately, even if a delta sync would often be sufficient in an already-established environment.\
\
**Learn more:** [Microsoft Entra Connect Sync: Scheduler](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-sync-feature-scheduler) · [Start-ADSyncSyncCycle](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/reference-connect-adsync#start-adsyncsynccycle)

You need to verify whether the issue is related to the NSGs.  
  
What should you use?

You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that contains an Azure virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 is connected to your on-premises network by using Azure ExpressRoute.  
  
You plan to prepare the environment for automatic failover if ExpressRoute fails.  
  
You need to connect VNet1 to the on-premises network by using a site-to-site VPN. The solution must minimize cost.  
  
Which three actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Create a local site VPN gateway
Create a VPN gateway that uses the VpnGw1 SKU
Create a VPN gateway that uses the Basic SKU

questions.explanation:
Because VNet1 already connects to on-premises over ExpressRoute, it already has a GatewaySubnet, and that same subnet is reused by the coexisting VPN gateway, so no additional gateway subnet needs to be created. ExpressRoute and site-to-site VPN coexistence is not supported on the Basic SKU, so the lowest-cost valid choice is a VPN gateway using the VpnGw1 SKU. To complete the path you also need a local network gateway representing the on-premises site and a connection resource linking the two gateways together.

**Learn more:** [Configure ExpressRoute and S2S VPN coexisting connections: Azure portal | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/how-to-configure-coexisting-gateway-portal)

You have an Azure subscription that contains a storage account named `storage1`.  
  
You plan to create a blob container named `container1`.  
  
You need to use customer-managed key encryption for `container1`.  
  
Which key should you use?

options.text: an EC key that uses the P-384 curve only
an EC key that uses the P-521 curve only
an EC key that uses the P-384 curve or P-521 curve only
an RSA key with a key size of 4096 only
an RSA key type with a key size of 2048, 3072, or 4096 only

questions.explanation:
Azure Storage customer-managed encryption supports only RSA or RSA-HSM keys in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM, with supported key sizes of 2048, 3072, or 4096 bits. EC keys are not supported for Azure Storage encryption, and 4096-bit RSA is valid but not the only valid size. Since a blob container uses the storage account’s encryption configuration, the correct key requirement is an RSA key type with a size of 2048, 3072, or 4096. Official documentation: Microsoft Learn, "Customer-managed keys for account encryption - Azure Storage."

**Learn more:** [Customer-managed keys for account encryption - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/customer-managed-keys-overview) · [Configure customer-managed keys in the same tenant for an existing storage account - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/customer-managed-keys-configure-existing-account)

Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor can generate log alerts from data stored in a Log Analytics workspace. If VM1 is connected to that workspace through the Microsoft Monitoring Agent and the workspace is configured to collect the Windows System event log, Azure Monitor can query those events and trigger an alert when the count of Error entries exceeds two within a 1-hour period. That matches the stated requirement.

questions.question:
Solution: You shut down VM1, and then add a new network interface to VM1.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
This does not meet the goal because an Azure VM can have multiple NICs only when the added NIC is in the same virtual network as the VM’s existing NIC. VM1 is connected to VNET1, but VNET2 is a different virtual network in a different region, so adding another NIC cannot attach VM1 directly to VNET2. Connecting VM1 to VNET2 would require network-to-network connectivity such as global virtual network peering, not just an extra NIC.\
\
**Learn more:** [Add network interfaces to or remove from Azure VMs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-network-interface-vm) · [Azure Virtual Network peering overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-peering-overview)

questions.question:
Solution: Delete VM1. Re-create VM1, and then create a new network interface for VM1 and connect it to VNET2.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: An Azure virtual machine cannot be moved directly from one virtual network to another due to architectural constraints—the VNet is determined at VM creation. The only supported approach is to delete the VM and recreate it with a network interface attached to the target VNet. Since the proposed solution explicitly performs this process (delete, recreate, and attach new NIC to VNET2), it correctly achieves the required connectivity to the new virtual network.

questions.question:
Solution: Delete VM1. Re-create VM1, and then create a new network interface for VM1 and connect it to VNET2.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
This does not meet the goal because moving VM1 to another resource group does not move it to another region. VM1 would still be in West US, while VNET2 is in East Asia. In Azure, a network interface attached to a virtual machine must be in the same location as the VM, and multiple NICs on a VM must be connected to subnets in the same virtual network. Since VM1 cannot attach a NIC from a VNet in a different region, it cannot be connected directly to VNET2 this way.

**Learn more:** [Add network interfaces to or remove from Azure VMs | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-network-interface-vm) · [Create and manage Windows VMs in Azure that use multiple NICs - Azure Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/multiple-nics)

questions.question:
Solution: You create a new network interface, and then you add the network interface to VM1.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Adding a network interface to an Azure virtual machine does not connect that VM to a different virtual network in another region. Azure requires the NICs attached to a VM to be in the same virtual network, and a multi-NIC VM can span multiple subnets only within that same VNet. Because VM1 is in West US on VNET1 and VNET2 is in East Asia, the required cross-VNet connectivity would need a feature such as global virtual network peering instead of an added NIC.\
\
**Learn more:** [Add network interfaces to or remove network interfaces from virtual machines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-network-interface-vm) · [Create and manage Windows VMs in Azure that use multiple NICs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/multiple-nics)

Solution: You create a new network interface, and then you add the network interface to VM1.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure Monitor alerts on Windows guest event logs require the VM's event data to be collected into Azure Monitor, typically by using Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule that sends Windows Event Log entries to Log Analytics, where a log alert can count matching error events within a one-hour window. Creating an event subscription on the VM does not provide the required Azure Monitor guest event log collection path, so this solution does not meet the requirement.

**Learn more:** [Collect Windows events from virtual machines with Azure Monitor Agent - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/vm/data-collection-windows-events) · [Monitor virtual machines with Azure Monitor: Alerts - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/vm/monitor-virtual-machine-alerts)

Solution: You create an Azure Log Analytics workspace and configure the Agent configuration settings. You install the Microsoft Monitoring Agent on VM1. You create an alert in Azure Monitor and specify the Log Analytics workspace as the source.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Collecting Windows System event log entries from VM1 into a Log Analytics workspace and then creating an Azure Monitor log alert on that workspace is a valid way to trigger an alert when the number of matching Error events exceeds a threshold within a 1-hour period. Microsoft Learn documents that guest event logs are collected into a Log Analytics workspace through an agent, and Azure Monitor supports log search alerts for data stored in that workspace. The Microsoft Monitoring Agent method is legacy today, but it still represents a solution that meets the requirement described here.

**Learn more:** [Azure Monitor alerts overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-overview) · [Log Analytics workspace overview - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/logs/log-analytics-workspace-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Solution: You create an Azure Storage account and configure shared access signatures (SASs). You install the Microsoft Monitoring Agent on VM1. You create an alert in Azure Monitor and specify the storage account as the source.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Windows Event Log entries from a VM must be collected into Azure Monitor Logs, where they can be queried from the `Event` table and evaluated by a log alert rule. Azure Monitor alerts use metric or log data sources in the Azure Monitor platform, and guest event-log alerting for VMs is based on log data sent to a Log Analytics workspace, not a storage account secured with SAS. Because the proposed alert uses the storage account as the source instead of Log Analytics/Azure Monitor Logs, it does not satisfy the requirement.

You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783632890844-hllch3x3.png)  
  
You need to create a network interface named NIC1.  
  
In which location can you create NIC1?

options.text: East US and North Europe only
East US, West Europe, and North Europe
East US and West Europe only

questions.explanation: An Azure network interface must be created in the same region as the virtual network subnet to which it will attach. Because the only listed virtual network, VNET1, is in East US, NIC1 can be created only in East US. The public IP in West Europe and the route table in North Europe do not allow the NIC to be created in those regions, because cross-region attachment to the East US virtual network is not supported for a NIC.

questions.question:
Your company has an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) subscription.  
  
You need to deploy five virtual machines (VMs) to your company's virtual network subnet.  
  
Each VM will have both a public IP address and a private IP address. Inbound and outbound security rules for all of these virtual machines must be identical.  
  
Which option represents the minimum number of network interfaces required for this configuration?
questions.explanation: In Azure, each virtual machine needs at least one network interface, and a single network interface can include a private IP configuration and be associated with a public IP address. The requirement for identical inbound and outbound security rules does not require extra interfaces, because those rules can be applied consistently by using network security groups on the NICs or subnet. For five VMs, the minimum is therefore one NIC per VM, for a total of five.

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription that includes two peered virtual networks named VNet1 and VNet2.  
  
You have a Network Virtual Appliance (NVA) named NetVA1.  
  
You need to ensure that traffic from VNet1 to VNet2 is inspected by using NetVA1.  
  
What should you use?

options.text: a route table that has custom routes

questions.explanation:
A route table with custom user-defined routes can override the peering system route for VNet2’s address prefix and set NetVA1 as the virtual-appliance next hop. This service-chaining configuration forces traffic from VNet1 to VNet2 through the NVA for inspection.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Virtual Network Peering](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-peering-overview) · [Azure virtual network traffic routing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-udr-overview)

options.text: Create Azure Management Groups for each department.
Create a resource group for each department.
Assign tags to the virtual machines.
Modify the settings of the virtual machines.

questions.explanation: Azure tags are the standard way to classify and organize Azure resources by using key-value metadata such as `Department=Sales` or `Department=HR`. Tags can be applied directly to virtual machines, allowing resources in the same resource group to be associated with different departments without restructuring subscriptions or resource groups. Management groups organize subscriptions, not individual VMs, and changing VM settings does not provide this kind of organizational labeling.

You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that contains a virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 is in a resource group named RG1.  
  
Subscription1 has a user named User1. User1 has the following roles:  
  
- Reader  
- Security Admin  
- Security Reader  
  
You need to make sure that User1 can assign the Reader role for VNet1 to other users.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Remove User1 from the Security Reader role for Subscription1. Assign User1 the Contributor role for RG1.
Assign User1 the Access Administrator role for VNet1.
Remove User1 from the Security Reader and Reader roles for Subscription1. Assign User1 the Contributor role for Subscription1.
Assign User1 the Network Contributor role for RG1.

questions.explanation:
Assigning Azure roles requires permission to manage access at the target scope, specifically the ability to create role assignments. The built-in **User Access Administrator** role provides that capability, while **Reader**, **Security Admin**, **Security Reader**, **Contributor**, and **Network Contributor** do not grant permission to assign Azure RBAC roles. Because the requirement is only for **VNet1**, granting that access at the **VNet1** scope is sufficient and follows least privilege.

**Learn more:** [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles) · [Assign Azure roles using the Azure portal - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/role-assignments-portal)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains a policy-based virtual network gateway named **GW1** and a virtual network named **VNet1**.  
  
You need to ensure that you can configure a point-to-site connection from an on-premises computer to **VNet1**.  
  
Which **two** actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Add a service endpoint to VNet1
Create a route-based virtual network gateway
Add a public IP address space to VNet1

questions.explanation:
Azure point-to-site VPN requires a **route-based** VPN gateway; a **policy-based** virtual network gateway does not support point-to-site connections. To enable P2S for VNet1, the existing policy-based gateway must be removed and replaced with a route-based virtual network gateway. Microsoft Learn states that point-to-site configurations require a route-based VPN type, and Azure guidance for remote work scenarios starts with creating a virtual network gateway and then configuring point-to-site on that gateway.

**Learn more:** [About Azure Point-to-Site VPN connections - Azure VPN Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/point-to-site-about) · [Remote work and point-to-site VPN gateways - Azure VPN Gateway](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/vpn-gateway/work-remotely-support)

What should you do?

options.text: Configure a conditional forwarder on VM1
Add service endpoints on VNET2 and VNET3
Configure peering between VNET1, VNET2, and VNET3

questions.explanation:
Azure can use a custom DNS server for name resolution across multiple virtual networks, but the VMs must be able to reach that DNS server over the network. Virtual network peering provides connectivity between VNets, while service endpoints do not provide VNet-to-VNet communication, and a conditional forwarder on VM1 does not solve reachability from other VNets. Microsoft Learn also states that resolving names across virtual networks requires a custom DNS server, and that peering alone does not provide cross-VNet name resolution unless you use your own DNS or Azure Private DNS.

**Learn more:** [Create, change, or delete an Azure virtual network - Azure Virtual Network](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/manage-virtual-network) · [Create, Change, or Delete Azure Virtual Network Peering](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-manage-peering)

questions.explanation: ARM template deployments are tracked in a resource group's deployment history. questions.explanation:
The exact ARM template used for a deployment is reviewed from the resource group's **Deployments** history, where Azure lets you open a specific deployment and view its **Template**. A blob container's Container blade manages storage container contents and settings, not ARM deployment templates, so it does not satisfy the requirement to review the template Jon Ross used.\

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You are deploying an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster that will contain multiple pods. The pods will use **kubenet** networking.  
  
You need to restrict network traffic between the pods.  
  
What should you configure on the AKS cluster?
questions.explanation:
Restricting traffic between AKS pods is done with a network policy engine. When the cluster uses **kubenet**, the supported choice for pod traffic control is **Calico network policy**. Azure network policy is not the correct fit for kubenet, while pod security policies control pod security settings rather than network flows, and application security groups apply to Azure virtual network resources instead of Kubernetes pod-to-pod traffic controls.

**Learn more:** [Secure Pod Traffic with Network Policies in Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/use-network-policies) · [Configure kubenet networking in Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/configure-kubenet)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that contains a virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 is in a resource group named RG1.  
  
Subscription1 has a user named User1. User1 has the following roles:  
  
- Reader  
- Security Admin  
- Security Reader  
  
You need to ensure that User1 can assign the Reader role for VNet1 to other users.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Assign User1 the Network Contributor role for VNet1.
Remove User1 from the Security Reader role for Subscription1. Assign User1 the Contributor role for RG1.
Assign User1 the Owner role for VNet1.
Assign User1 the Network Contributor role for RG1.

questions.explanation:
Assigning an Azure RBAC role requires the `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` permission at the target scope. The Owner role includes the ability to manage all resources and assign roles in Azure RBAC, while Contributor and Network Contributor do not allow role assignment. Therefore, assigning User1 the Owner role on VNet1 enables User1 to grant the Reader role for that virtual network.

**Learn more:** [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles) · [Assign Azure roles using the Azure portal - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/role-assignments-portal)

questions.explanation:
A resource group deletion fails if any contained resource can't be deleted. A resource with a **Delete** lock must have that lock removed before deletion, and a **Recovery Services vault** can't be deleted while it still contains backup items or backup data. Because **VNET1** is protected by a delete lock and **Vault1** contains backups of **VM1**, you must remove the lock from **VNET1** and delete the backup data in **Vault1** before the resource group can be deleted.

**Learn more:** [Delete a Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Vault - Azure Backup](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-azure-delete-vault) · [Delete Resource Groups and Resources - Azure Resource Manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/delete-resource-group)

You have an Azure subscription containing three virtual machines named VM1, VM2, and VM3. All of the virtual machines are in an availability set named AVSet1.  
  
You need to scale up VM1 to a new virtual machine size, but that size is unavailable.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Convert AvSet1 into a managed availability set.

questions.explanation: Deallocating the virtual machine releases its compute allocation, allowing Azure to place it on hardware that supports the requested VM size. A guest OS shutdown does not release the Azure compute allocation, and proximity placement groups or availability-set management changes do not make an unavailable size available.

questions.question:
You have an app named App1 that runs on two Azure virtual machines named VM1 and VM2.  
  
You plan to implement an Azure Availability Set for App1. The solution must ensure that App1 remains available during planned maintenance of the hardware hosting VM1 and VM2.  
  
What should you include in the Availability Set?
questions.explanation: In an Azure Availability Set, **update domains** separate virtual machines so that planned maintenance is performed on only one domain at a time. To keep an application running across two VMs during planned maintenance, the VMs must be distributed across at least **two update domains**. Fault domains are intended for protection from unplanned physical hardware failures, not planned maintenance.

You plan to implement an Azure Availability Set for App1. The solution must ensure that App1 remains available during planned maintenance of the hardware hosting VM1 and VM2.

the subnets on VNet1, VNet2, and VNet3

questions.explanation:
A network security group can be associated with subnet resources, including multiple subnets, but the subnet's virtual network must be in the same Azure region as the NSG. Because NSG1 is in **East US**, it can be associated only with subnets in **VNet3**, which is also in **East US**. The resource group does not restrict this association.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to create an Azure Storage account named `storage1`. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Support Azure Data Lake Storage.  
- Minimize costs for infrequently accessed data.  
- Automatically replicate data to a secondary Azure region.  
  
Which three options should you configure for `storage1`? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct answer is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 requires **hierarchical namespace** to be enabled on the storage account. For data that is accessed infrequently, the **Cool** access tier reduces storage cost compared to the Hot tier. Replication to a secondary Azure region requires **geo-redundant storage (GRS)**, because ZRS provides zone-level replication only within the primary region. Official Microsoft documentation describes hierarchical namespace as the core Data Lake capability, the Cool tier as optimized for infrequently accessed data, and GRS as the option that asynchronously copies data to a paired secondary region.

**Learn more:** [Azure Data Lake Storage hierarchical namespace - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/data-lake-storage-namespace) · [Access tiers for blob data - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/access-tiers-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that includes the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783640519330-5u2n9qmv.png)  
  
You configure Azure Site Recovery to replicate VM1 between the East US and West US Azure regions.  
  
You run a test failover of VM1 and specify VNET2 as the target virtual network.  
  
When the test instance of VM1 is created, which subnet will the virtual machine connect to?
questions.explanation:
VM1 is connected to Subnet2 (172.16.2.0/24) in VNET1, and VNET2 has no subnet named "Subnet2" - its subnets are DemoSubnet1, RecoverySubnetA, RecoverySubnetB, and TestSubnet1. Azure Site Recovery only auto-matches a test-failover VM to a target subnet with the identical name; when no name match exists, it falls back to selecting the first subnet in alphabetical order, which here is DemoSubnet1 (ahead of RecoverySubnetA, RecoverySubnetB, and TestSubnet1). Address-range matching (which would suggest TestSubnet1, also 172.16.2.0/24) is not how ASR performs this fallback.

**Learn more:** [Run a test failover in Azure Site Recovery](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/site-recovery/site-recovery-test-failover-to-azure)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have five Azure virtual machines that run Windows Server 2016. The virtual machines are configured as web servers.  
  
You have an Azure load balancer named LB1 that provides load-balancing services for the virtual machines.  
  
You need to ensure that visitors are served by the same web server for each request.  
  
What should you configure?

options.text: Session persistence to Client IP and protocol

questions.explanation:
Azure Load Balancer uses session persistence to keep requests from the same client directed to the same backend instance. The **Client IP and protocol** setting applies source IP affinity based on the client IP address and protocol, so successive requests from the same client and protocol combination are handled by the same virtual machine. A health probe only checks whether instances are healthy, and idle timeout does not control server affinity.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer distribution modes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/distribution-mode-concepts) · [Configure Azure Load Balancer distribution mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-distribution-mode)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to create an Azure Storage account named `storage1` that will contain a file share named `share1`.  
  
You need to ensure that `share1` can support SMB Multichannel. The solution must minimize costs.  
  
How should you configure storage?
questions.explanation:
Azure Files supports SMB Multichannel only on SSD file shares, which requires **Premium** performance. Premium Azure file shares support **LRS or ZRS**, but not GRS. To minimize cost while still meeting the SMB Multichannel requirement, **Premium performance with locally-redundant storage (LRS)** is the correct choice.

**Learn more:** [SMB File Shares in Azure Files](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/files/files-smb-protocol) · [Data Redundancy in Azure Files](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/files/files-redundancy)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783637504177-q3snls16.png)  
  
The **Not allowed resource types** Azure Policy, with policy enforcement enabled, is assigned to **RG1** and uses the following parameters:  
  
- `Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks`  
- `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines`  
  
In **RG1**, you need to create a new virtual machine named **VM2**, and then connect **VM2** to **VNET1**.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Create an Azure Resource Manager template

questions.explanation:
A policy using the **Not allowed resource types** definition denies creation of any resource types listed in its parameters when enforcement is enabled. Because **VM2** is a `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines` resource, its creation in **RG1** will be blocked until that resource type is removed from the policy assignment parameters. The existing virtual network **VNET1** does not require creating a new `Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks` resource just to attach the VM to it, so removing the virtual network type from the policy is not the necessary first step. citeturn0search0turn0search1

questions.question:
Your company has an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) subscription.  
  
You need to deploy five virtual machines (VMs) to your company's virtual network subnet.  
  
Each VM will have both a public IP address and a private IP address.  
  
Inbound and outbound security rules for all of these virtual machines must be identical.  
  
Which of the following is the minimum number of security groups required for this configuration?
questions.explanation: In Azure, a Network Security Group (NSG) contains inbound and outbound security rules and can be assigned at the subnet level so that the same rules apply to every virtual machine in that subnet. Because all five VMs require identical rules and are being deployed to the same subnet, one NSG applied to that subnet is sufficient. The presence of both public and private IP addresses on each VM does not require additional security groups.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription. The subscription contains virtual machines that connect to a virtual network named VNet1.  
  
You plan to configure Azure Monitor for VM Insights.  
  
You need to ensure that all the virtual machines communicate with Azure Monitor only through VNet1.  
  
What should you create first?

options.text: an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS)

questions.explanation:
To keep VM Insights traffic private over VNet1, Azure Monitor must use Azure Private Link. The Azure Monitor private link setup begins by creating an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS), which defines the monitoring boundary and is the resource that later gets connected to a private endpoint. A private endpoint is created afterward, while a Log Analytics workspace or a data collection rule does not by itself force Azure Monitor communication to remain on the virtual network. Official guidance for configuring private link for Azure Monitor lists the sequence as: create AMPLS, connect Azure Monitor resources to it, and then connect AMPLS to a private endpoint.

**Learn more:** [Configure private link for Azure Monitor - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/fundamentals/private-link-configure) · [Use Azure Private Link to connect networks to Azure Monitor - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/fundamentals/private-link-security)

In Azure virtual network peering, **Allow gateway transit** must be enabled on the virtual network that **has** the VPN gateway, and the peered virtual network must enable **Use remote gateways** to consume that gateway. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1. Subscription1 contains the resource groups shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783630940670-sydrauv1.png)  
  
RG1 contains a web app named WebApp1. WebApp1 is located in West Europe.  
  
You move WebApp1 to RG2.  
  
What is the effect of the move?

options.text: The App Service plan for WebApp1 remains in West Europe. Policy2 applies to WebApp1.
The App Service plan for WebApp1 moves to North Europe. Policy2 applies to WebApp1.
The App Service plan for WebApp1 remains in West Europe. Policy1 applies to WebApp1.
The App Service plan for WebApp1 moves to North Europe. Policy1 applies to WebApp1.

questions.explanation:
Moving WebApp1 to a different resource group changes its resource group scope, not its Azure region. The app and its App Service plan remain in West Europe unless the app is explicitly moved to another App Service plan, which is a separate operation. Azure Policy is inherited from the scope where it is assigned, including resource groups, so once WebApp1 is in RG2, the policy assigned to RG2 applies to it. Therefore, the App Service plan remains in West Europe and Policy2 applies.

**Learn more:** [Move Azure resources to a new resource group or subscription - Azure Resource Manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/move-resource-group-and-subscription) · [Manage an App Service Plan - Azure App Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/app-service-plan-manage)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have two Azure virtual machines named VM1 and VM2, and two Recovery Services vaults named RSV1 and RSV2.  
  
VM2 is backed up to RSV1.  
  
You need to back up VM2 to RSV2.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: From the RSV1 blade, click Backup items and stop the VM2 backup

questions.explanation:
An Azure virtual machine can be protected by only one Recovery Services vault at a time. Microsoft Learn guidance for Azure Backup says that to change the Recovery Services vault for a VM, you must stop the current backup first, and then configure backup in the new vault. Therefore the required first step is to stop VM2 backup in RSV1.

questions.question:
You have an Azure Storage account named `storage1` that contains a blob container named `container1`.  
  
You need to ensure that new content added to `container1` cannot be modified for one year.  
  
What should you configure?
questions.explanation: To stop newly written blobs from being changed for a defined period, Azure Blob Storage uses an immutable policy with time-based retention at the container scope. That policy enforces write-once, read-many behavior for new blobs for the specified retention interval, such as one year. Access tiers only control storage cost and retrieval characteristics, Access control (IAM) governs permissions rather than immutability enforcement, and access level controls public anonymous access. Therefore the matching choice is the container policy option.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a subnet named Subnet1 that contains Azure virtual machines. A network security group (NSG) named NSG1 is associated with Subnet1. NSG1 contains only the default rules.  
  
You need to create a rule in NSG1 to prevent the hosts on Subnet1 from connecting to the Azure portal. The hosts must still be able to connect to other internet hosts.  
  
To what should you set **Destination** in the rule?
questions.explanation:
In an Azure network security group rule, the **Destination** field can use a **service tag** to match traffic for a specific Azure service. Microsoft documents that NSG source and destination values support service tags, and service tags are used in security rules to allow or deny traffic for the corresponding service. Because the requirement is to block Azure portal traffic without blocking other Internet destinations, the destination should be configured as a **Service Tag** rather than **Any**, an application security group, or a generic IP-address-based target.

**Learn more:** [Azure service tags overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-nz/azure/virtual-network/service-tags-overview) · [Azure network security groups overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/%20azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning to deploy several Azure virtual machines that will run Windows Server 2019 in a virtual machine scale set by using an Azure Resource Manager template.  
  
You need to make sure that NGINX is available on all of the virtual machines after deployment.  
  
What should you use?

options.text: Deployment Center in Azure App Service
a Microsoft Intune device configuration profile

questions.explanation:
To ensure software is present on every instance in an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set, you use a VM extension that applies configuration inside the guest OS. The Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension is intended to deploy and enforce PowerShell DSC configurations on Azure VMs and VM scale sets, which can install and configure required components such as NGINX on Windows Server 2019. The other options target different services or management scenarios and do not fit ARM-template-based VM scale set software provisioning.

**Learn more:** [Azure Desired State Configuration extension](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/dsc-overview) · [Virtual machine scale sets overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains a storage account named `storageacct1234` and two users named `User1` and `User2`.  
  
You assign `User1` the roles shown in the following exhibit.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783637655175-qlhewgt8.jpg)  
  
Which two actions can `User1` perform? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Assign roles to User2 for storageacct1234.

questions.explanation:
The **Reader** role provides read-only access to the storage account's management plane, which lets a user view the resource but not change settings or assign roles. The **Storage Blob Data Contributor** role grants read, write, and delete access to Blob storage containers and blobs. Together, those roles allow access to blob data in the storage account, including uploading blobs and viewing blob data in the portal. They do not permit changing the storage account firewall, assigning RBAC roles to another user, or accessing Azure Files shares, which require different permissions or roles.

**Learn more:** [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles) · [Assign an Azure role for access to blob data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/assign-azure-role-data-access)

questions.question:
Your company has three virtual machines (VMs) that are part of an availability set.  
  
You attempt to resize one of the VMs, and an allocation failure message is returned.  
  
It is imperative that the VM be resized.  
  
Which action should you take?

options.text: You should only stop one of the VMs.
You should stop two of the VMs.
You should stop all three VMs.
You should remove the necessary VM from the availability set.

questions.explanation: When a VM in an availability set cannot be resized because of an allocation failure, Azure may not have capacity for the new size within the current cluster/placement constraints of that availability set. The supported remediation is to stop (deallocate) all VMs in the availability set and then retry, allowing Azure to reallocate the set together on infrastructure that can support the requested size.

You need to assign User1 a role that ensures the user can access the blob data in storage1. The role assignment must support conditions.  
  
Which two roles can you assign to User1? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
> NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
Azure role-assignment conditions for Blob Storage can be added to the built-in Storage Blob Data Contributor and Storage Blob Data Owner roles. Both roles include Blob Storage data permissions, so either role grants access to blob data while supporting a condition on that assignment.

**Learn more:** [Add or edit Azure role assignment conditions using the Azure portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/conditions-role-assignments-portal) · [Azure built-in roles](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles)

You have an Azure subscription that includes a user named User1.  
  
You need to ensure that User1 can deploy virtual machines and manage virtual networks. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which role-based access control (RBAC) role should you assign to User1?
questions.explanation: To deploy virtual machines and manage virtual networks while following the principle of least privilege, the Contributor role is the minimum required. Virtual Machine Contributor does not grant management access to virtual networks, making it insufficient for this combined requirement. Owner grants excessive permissions. Contributor is the least-privileged built-in role that encompasses both VM deployment and virtual network management capabilities.

You need to make sure that ContReg1 supports geo-replication.

You should restore the VM to any VM within the company's subscription.
You should restore the VM to a new Azure VM.
You should restore the VM to an on-premise Windows device.

questions.explanation:
Azure Backup restore for an Azure VM is performed by creating a restored VM in Azure from a selected recovery point, and Microsoft ransomware guidance recommends recovering to a clean environment from a known safe point in time. Restoring to a new Azure VM isolates the recovered workload from the compromised instance and matches the supported VM restore workflow for Azure IaaS backups.

**Learn more:** [Restore VMs by using the Azure portal using Azure Backup - Azure Backup | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-azure-arm-restore-vms) · [About the Azure Virtual Machine restore process - Azure Backup | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/about-azure-vm-restore)

You plan to export data by using an Azure Import/Export job named Export1.  
  
You need to determine which data can be exported by using Export1.  
  
Which data should you identify?
questions.explanation:
Azure Import/Export export jobs can export data only from Azure Blob storage. Export of Azure Files isn't supported, and Azure SQL Database and Azure Table storage aren't supported by this service for export jobs. Therefore, the only eligible item listed is the blob container named container1.

**Learn more:** [Requirements for Azure Import/Export service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/import-export/storage-import-export-requirements) · [Using Azure Import/Export to transfer data to and from Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/import-export/storage-import-export-service)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a general-purpose v1 Azure Storage account named `storage1` that uses locally-redundant storage (LRS).  
  
You need to ensure that the data in the storage account is protected if a zone fails. The solution must minimize costs and administrative effort.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Upgrade the account to general-purpose v2.
Modify the Replication setting of storage1.

questions.explanation:
Protection against an availability zone failure requires zone-redundant storage (ZRS). For this scenario, the blocking constraint is the account type: a general-purpose v1 storage account must be upgraded to general-purpose v2 before using the current ZRS redundancy model. Upgrading the existing account is the least expensive and lowest-effort first action because it avoids creating and migrating to a new storage account. Microsoft Learn documents that standard general-purpose v2 (`StorageV2`) is the recommended account type for ZRS and that v1 accounts should be upgraded when changing redundancy scenarios.

**Learn more:** [Data redundancy - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-redundancy) · [Change how a storage account is replicated - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/redundancy-migration)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are setting up Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) authentication for an Azure Storage account named `storage1`.  
  
You need to ensure that the members of a group named `Group1` can upload files by using the Azure portal. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.  
  
Which two roles should you configure for `storage1`? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
For Azure portal access to blob data with Microsoft Entra authentication, users need both an Azure Resource Manager role to view and navigate the storage account and a blob data role to perform data operations. The least-privilege management role is **Reader**, which allows the storage account to be accessed in the portal without broader administrative rights. To upload files, the required data role is **Storage Blob Data Contributor**, which grants read/write/delete access to containers and blobs. Broader roles such as Contributor or Storage Account Contributor exceed least-privilege requirements, and Storage Blob Data Reader does not allow uploads.

**Learn more:** [Assign an Azure role for access to blob data - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/assign-azure-role-data-access) · [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles)

You deploy Azure virtual machines to three Azure regions.  
  
Each region contains a virtual network. Each virtual network contains multiple subnets peered in a full mesh topology.  
  
Each subnet contains a network security group (NSG) that has defined rules.  
  
A user reports that they cannot use port 33000 to connect from a virtual machine in one region to a virtual machine in another region.  
  
Which two options can you use to diagnose the issue? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
Azure Network Watcher **IP flow verify** can test whether traffic to or from a VM on a specified protocol and port is allowed or denied by the effective NSG configuration, and it identifies the rule responsible. **Connection troubleshoot** can test end-to-end connectivity between Azure resources, including VM-to-VM communication on a specified TCP port, which makes it suitable for diagnosing why port 33000 fails between regions. These two tools directly diagnose blocked or failed VM connectivity, whereas the other options are not the primary complete troubleshooting methods for this scenario.

**Learn more:** [Quickstart: Diagnose a virtual machine network traffic filter problem using the Azure portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/diagnose-vm-network-traffic-filtering-problem) · [Troubleshoot outbound connections](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/connection-troubleshoot-manage)

questions.question:
Solution: On Subscription1, you assign the **DevTest Labs User** role to the **Developers** group.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: The **DevTest Labs User** built-in Azure role is scoped to working with **DevTest Labs** resources and does not provide the general write permissions needed to create **Azure Logic Apps** in a resource group. To create Logic Apps, the group would need a role that includes appropriate `Microsoft.Logic` write permissions, such as **Contributor** at the resource-group scope.

questions.question:
Solution: On Subscription1, you assign the **Logic App Operator** role to the **Developers** group.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
The Logic App Operator role does not include permission to create Logic Apps. Microsoft documents this role as allowing operational access such as reading, enabling, and disabling logic apps, while creation and management require a role with write permissions, such as Logic App Contributor or Contributor. Because the requirement is to let the Developers group create Azure Logic Apps in the Dev resource group, assigning Logic App Operator does not satisfy that requirement.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles) · [Secure access and data in workflows - Azure Logic Apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/logic-apps/logic-apps-securing-a-logic-app)

questions.question:
Solution: You assign the **Contributor** role to the **Developers** group on **Dev**.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: The Azure built-in Contributor role allows users to create and manage all types of Azure resources at the assigned scope, including resources in a resource group such as Azure Logic Apps. Because the assignment is made on the Dev resource group, the Developers group can create Logic Apps in that resource group, which fulfills the stated requirement.

questions.question:
Solution: On **Dev**, you assign the **Logic App Contributor** role to the **Developers** group.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
The Logic App Contributor built-in Azure RBAC role allows creating and managing Logic Apps. When that role is assigned at the Dev resource group scope, members of the Developers group can create Logic App resources in that resource group, which satisfies the stated requirement.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure built-in roles for Integration - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles/integration) · [Secure access and data in workflows - Azure Logic Apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/logic-apps/logic-apps-securing-a-logic-app)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Solution: You assign a built-in policy definition to the subscription.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Assigning a built-in Azure Policy at the subscription level does not by itself guarantee that newly created network security groups will receive a rule that blocks TCP port 8080 between virtual networks. Azure Policy can enforce or deploy configuration only when an appropriate policy definition exists, and Microsoft’s built-in Azure networking policy set does not include a built-in definition for automatically creating that specific NSG deny rule. Because the requirement is automatic enforcement of a particular NSG rule, this solution is insufficient.

**Learn more:** [Built-in policy definitions for Azure networking services](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/policy-reference) · [Azure Policy definitions effect basics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/policy/concepts/effect-basics)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Solution: From the **Resource providers** blade, you unregister the **Microsoft.ClassicNetwork** provider.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Unregistering **Microsoft.ClassicNetwork** only affects the legacy classic networking resource provider and does not configure or enforce rules on Azure Resource Manager network security groups. To automatically block TCP port 8080 between virtual networks when NSGs are created, you would need an NSG rule and typically a governance mechanism such as Azure Policy or deployment automation to require that rule. Microsoft documentation for NSGs shows that traffic filtering is performed by NSG security rules, including deny rules by port and source such as `VirtualNetwork`; it is not controlled by unregistering a resource provider.

**Learn more:** [How Network Security Groups Filter Network Traffic in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-group-how-it-works) · [Check Security Rules Using NSG Diagnostics - Azure Network Watcher](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/diagnose-network-security-rules)

questions.question:
Solution: You create a resource lock, and then assign the lock to the subscription.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure resource locks are governance controls that protect resources from deletion or modification, but they do not configure newly created network security groups with specific security rules. To ensure every new NSG automatically blocks TCP port 8080 between virtual networks, you would need policy-based enforcement, not a subscription-level resource lock.\
\
**Learn more:** [Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure - Azure Resource Manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/lock-resources) · [Network security groups and application security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/network-application-security-groups)

questions.question:
Solution: You configure a custom policy definition, and then assign the policy to the subscription.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
A custom Azure Policy assigned at the subscription scope can enforce required NSG configuration for newly created network security groups. questions.explanation:
For a Microsoft Entra joined device, local administrator rights are granted to the user who joins the device and to users in the Global Administrator role. The setting for additional local administrators controls the Microsoft Entra Joined Device Local Administrator role; when it is set to **None**, that role adds nobody. Therefore **User1** is a local administrator because they joined Computer1, **User2** is a local administrator because they are a Global administrator, **User3** is not added because no additional local administrators are configured, and **User4** is not added because the Intune administrator role does not make a user a local administrator on the device.

**Learn more:** [How to manage local administrators on Microsoft Entra joined devices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/devices/assign-local-admin)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.

What should you do?
questions.explanation:
Application security groups are used by adding a network interface's IP configuration to the ASG, so the VM becomes part of that logical group through its NIC. Microsoft Learn states that application security groups group network interfaces by role, and Azure network interface configuration supports setting application security group membership on the NIC/IP configuration. Therefore, to apply ASG1 to VM1, you associate NIC1 with ASG1.

**Learn more:** [Network security groups and application security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/network-application-security-groups) · [Create, change, or delete Azure network interfaces](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-network-interface)

Solution: You create a new Multi-Factor Authentication provider by using a backup of the existing Multi-Factor Authentication provider data.  
  
Does this solution meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
An Azure Multi-Factor Authentication provider's usage model cannot be changed after the provider is created. To move from **Per Authentication** to **Per Enabled User**, you must create a new MFA provider that uses the required model, then reuse or restore the existing MFA Server data with that new provider. That is why this solution meets the stated requirement.

**Learn more:** [Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication providers - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-mfa-authprovider) · [How to use the MFA Server Migration Utility to migrate to Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/how-to-mfa-server-migration-utility)

questions.question:
Solution: Reconfigure the current usage model by using the Azure portal.  
  
Does the solution meet the goal?
questions.explanation: Once a Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) provider is created in Azure, its usage model cannot be changed through the Azure portal or any other configuration method. Changing from Per Authentication to Per Enabled User billing model requires creating a new MFA provider with the desired configuration. This limitation reflects Azure's architecture where the usage model is tied to the provider resource type, not a modifiable setting.

questions.question:
Solution: You use the Azure CLI to reconfigure the existing usage model.  
  
Does this solution achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Changing the MFA provider usage model from **Per Authentication** to **Per Enabled User** is a billing/configuration change, not the step that enables the newly added employees to use multifactor authentication. Per-user MFA must be enabled for those accounts, or MFA must be enforced through modern Microsoft Entra controls such as Conditional Access. Microsoft Learn distinguishes MFA provider billing models from the separate per-user MFA enablement states for user accounts.\
\
**Learn more:** [Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication FAQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/authentication/multi-factor-authentication-faq) · [Enable per-user multifactor authentication - Microsoft Entra ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/howto-mfa-userstates)

one Availability Set that has three fault domains and one update domain

one virtual machine scale set that has 12 virtual machines instances

questions.explanation:
Azure planned maintenance is performed one update domain at a time for highly available VM deployments. Availability Sets use update domains, and Virtual Machine Scale Sets are also maintained in update-domain or batch boundaries rather than all instances at once. For this requirement, the expected design is a single VM scale set sized so that maintenance of one update domain still leaves at least eight instances available. With the exam’s standard five update domains for a scale set, 10 instances provide two instances per update domain, so losing one update domain during planned maintenance still leaves eight running.

**Learn more:** [Availability sets overview - Azure Virtual Machines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/availability-set-overview) · [Planned maintenance notifications for Virtual Machine Scale Sets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-maintenance-notifications)

questions.question:
Solution: Set **Admin user** to **Enable** for Registry1.  
  
Does this accomplish the goal?
questions.explanation:
Enabling an Azure Container Registry admin user makes registry credentials available for authenticating image pulls. The admin account is required when deploying an image directly from Azure Container Registry to Azure Container Instances through the Azure portal.\
\
**Learn more:** [Deploy to Azure Container Instances from Azure Container Registry using a service principal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-using-azure-container-registry) · [Azure Container Registry authentication options](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-authentication)

Solution: Assign the **AcrPull** role for Registry1 to ACR-Tasks-Network.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
The AcrPull role authorizes the assigned security principal to pull images from the registry. Assigning it to the ACR Tasks managed identity does not authorize a separate Azure Container Instance to pull the image; the container instance must use authorized registry credentials or its own configured managed identity with the required pull permission.\
\
**Learn more:** [Deploy to Azure Container Instances from Azure Container Registry using a managed identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/using-azure-container-registry-mi) · [Managed Identity in ACR Task](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-tasks-authentication-managed-identity)

Enabling them alone does not configure Azure Container Instances with the required registry authentication or managed identity permissions to pull an image, so it does not by itself resolve a container-instance deployment error.\

The container deployment still requires registry authentication and pull permission, such as a managed identity or service principal assigned the appropriate pull role.\
\
**Learn more:** [Deploy to Azure Container Instances from Azure Container Registry using a managed identity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/using-azure-container-registry-mi) · [Authenticate with Azure Container Registry from Azure Container Instances](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-auth-aci)

Because User2's Global Administrator role is stated only for the original tenant and not for `external.contoso.onmicrosoft.com`, User2 would not automatically be able to create user accounts there. `New-AzureADUser` is for creating regular users in the directory, not for inviting external B2B guest users. To provision external users as guests, Microsoft Entra uses the guest invitation process, which creates a user of type Guest and supports redemption by the external identity. Official Microsoft documentation separates **create a new user** from **invite an external guest**, and the PowerShell method for this scenario uses invitation cmdlets rather than `New-AzureADUser`.

**Learn more:** [How to create, invite, and delete users in Microsoft Entra ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/how-to-create-delete-users?view=gestures-1.0) · [Quickstart: Add a guest user and send an invitation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/external-id/b2b-quickstart-add-guest-users-portal)

Does this meet the goal?

Creating an invitation creates a guest user account in the tenant, and Microsoft documents bulk guest invitation by processing users from a CSV with PowerShell. Because the requirement is to create a guest account for each of the 500 external users, running that cmdlet once per user satisfies the goal.\

For B2B collaboration, submitting the CSV starts a bulk operation that adds the invitations and creates the guest user accounts in the directory, so it satisfies the requirement to create guest accounts for 500 external users.\

Microsoft’s bulk guest-user guidance for CSV-based onboarding uses invitations rather than `New-MgUser`. Therefore, a script that runs `New-MgUser` for each external user does not meet the requirement.\

Therefore, a script for these 500 external users should use the invitation cmdlet/API, such as `New-MgInvitation`, rather than `New-MgUser`.\

questions.explanation:
For a Standard Azure Load Balancer, backend virtual machines cannot use Basic SKU public IPs. Microsoft Learn states that Basic public IPs are not supported on Standard Load Balancer, and that a VM or NIC can reference only one SKU type, never both. Assigning Standard SKU public IP addresses to the VMs removes the Basic/Standard SKU conflict, so VM1 and VM2 can be added to the backend pool of the Standard internal load balancer.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer SKUs | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/skus) · [Upgrade public IP addresses attached to a VM from Basic to Standard - Azure Virtual Network | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/public-ip-upgrade-vm)

questions.question:
Solution: You remove the public IP address association from the network interface of VM2.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
This meets the goal because a Standard Load Balancer backend pool can't include a VM NIC that is associated with a Basic SKU public IP address. Removing VM2's Basic public IP eliminates that incompatibility, and VM1 already has no public IP. Standard Load Balancer backend pools can contain VM network interfaces in the virtual network without requiring a public IP on the VM.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer portal settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/manage) · [Azure Load Balancer components](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/components)

questions.question:
Solution: You create a **Basic SKU** public IP address, associate the address with the network interface of **VM1**, and then start **VM1**.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: A Standard SKU Azure Load Balancer cannot have backend pool members whose network interfaces are associated with Basic SKU public IP addresses. Creating a Basic public IP for VM1 makes VM1 ineligible, and VM2 already has a Basic public IP, so the requirement to add both VM1 and VM2 to the backend pool of LB1 is still not met. Starting VM1 only addresses its stopped state, not the Basic-versus-Standard SKU compatibility requirement.

questions.question:
Solution: You create a Standard SKU public IP address, associate the address to the network interface of VM1, and then stop VM2.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
A Standard internal Azure Load Balancer can use backend NICs from the same virtual network, and the backend VM does not need a public IP address. The actual incompatibility here is VM2's Basic SKU public IP. Stopping VM2 does not change or remove that Basic public IP, so VM2 remains ineligible for the Standard Load Balancer backend pool. Adding a Standard public IP to VM1 is unnecessary and does not resolve VM2's SKU mismatch.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer SKUs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/load-balancer/skus) · [Azure Load Balancer components](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/components)

Which FQDN will be returned?
questions.explanation:
With Azure-provided DNS, Azure automatically registers VM private IP addresses with internal forward and reverse DNS records. The Azure-managed PTR record for a VM’s private IP resolves to the VM name under the default internal suffix, `[vmname].internal.cloudapp.net`. Since `10.0.0.4` is assigned to VM1, the reverse lookup returns `vm1.internal.cloudapp.net`.

**Learn more:** [Azure Virtual Network Name Resolution Guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-name-resolution-for-vms-and-role-instances) · [Azure Private DNS FAQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/dns/dns-faq-private)

You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Stream Analytics job named Job1.  
  
You need to monitor the input events for Job1 to determine the number of events that were **not processed**.  
  
Which metric should you use?
questions.explanation: In Azure Stream Analytics, the **Late Input Events** metric tracks input events that are not processed because they arrive later than the job’s configured late-arrival tolerance. That directly identifies events that were dropped instead of being processed. By contrast, **Output Events** counts emitted results, **Out-of-Order Events** indicates ordering issues, and **Backlogged Input Events** shows events waiting to be processed rather than events discarded from processing.

In an ARM template, the resource is deployed using the value assigned to that resource's `location` property. Here the VM resource location is hard-coded as `westeurope`, so choosing a different deployment value or changing an unused variable will not change where the VM is created. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains 10 network security groups (NSGs), 10 virtual machines, and a Log Analytics workspace named Workspace1. Each NSG is connected to a virtual machine.  
  
You need to configure an Azure Monitor Network Insights alert that will be triggered when suspicious network traffic is detected.  
  
What should you do first?
questions.explanation:
Suspicious network traffic detection in Azure network monitoring relies on flow-log telemetry. NSG flow logs record IP traffic that passes through network security groups, and Azure traffic analytics/Network Insights use that flow data to surface security-relevant patterns and support alerting. Connection Monitor is for connectivity monitoring, while data collection endpoints and private link do not create the required network traffic log source. Although Microsoft now recommends virtual network flow logs for new deployments, the prerequisite represented by the available choices is NSG flow logs.

**Learn more:** [Network monitoring and observability | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/monitor) · [Manage NSG Flow Logs - Azure Network Watcher | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/nsg-flow-logs-manage)
