You need to configure a proximity placement group for VMSS1.  
  
Which proximity placement groups should you use?
questions.explanation:
A proximity placement group can be associated only with compute resources in the same Azure region. VMSS1 is located in **West US**, so it can use only a proximity placement group that is also in **West US**. Among the listed groups, only **Proximity1** matches that region; **Proximity2** and **Proximity3** are in **Central US** and cannot be assigned to VMSS1. Microsoft Learn states that proximity placement groups provide colocation within the same datacenter in a region and are set at the virtual machine scale set resource level.

**Learn more:** [Proximity placement groups - Azure Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/co-location) · [Proximity placement groups for Virtual Machine Scale Sets - Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/proximity-placement-groups)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have five Azure virtual machines that run Windows Server 2016. The virtual machines are configured as web servers.  
  
You have an Azure load balancer named LB1 that provides load-balancing services for the virtual machines.  
  
You need to ensure that visitors are served by the same web server for each request.  
  
What should you configure?

options.text: Session persistence to Client IP and protocol
Floating IP (direct server return) to Enabled

questions.explanation:
Azure Load Balancer session persistence provides source IP affinity so that successive requests from the same client are directed to the same backend instance. Microsoft Learn states that **Client IP and protocol** specifies that successive requests from the same client IP address and protocol combination are handled by the same virtual machine, which matches the requirement to keep a visitor on the same web server. Floating IP is unrelated to session stickiness, and None removes persistence.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer distribution modes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/distribution-mode-concepts) · [Configure Azure Load Balancer distribution mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-distribution-mode)

Azure Monitor Network Insights is designed to provide both an interactive topology view and detailed metrics dashboards for Azure networking resources. For ExpressRoute, Network Insights includes a functional dependency topology that shows components such as peerings, connections, and gateways, and it also provides a detailed preloaded metrics dashboard for availability, throughput, packet drops, and gateway metrics. That matches the need to visualize the network topology and display detailed metrics for VNet1's ExpressRoute connectivity.

**Learn more:** [Azure ExpressRoute Insights using Network Insights](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/expressroute/expressroute-network-insights) · [Network insights](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/network-insights-overview)

Your company has an Azure subscription that contains a Recovery Services vault.  
  
You want to use Azure Backup to schedule a backup of your company's virtual machines (VMs) to the Recovery Services vault.  
  
Which of the following VMs can you back up? **Choose all that apply.**

options.text: VMs that run Windows Server 2012 or higher.
VMs that have NOT been shut down.
VMs that have been shut down.

questions.explanation:
Azure Backup for Azure VMs supports 64-bit Windows Server operating systems (from Windows Server 2008 onward), 64-bit Windows 10 as a guest OS, and Debian 8.2+ among its endorsed Linux distributions. It can also back up a VM regardless of whether the VM is currently running or has been shut down, the only difference being that a shut-down VM produces a crash-consistent rather than an application-consistent recovery point. None of the listed VM configurations fall outside what Azure Backup can protect.

**Learn more:** [Support matrix for Azure VM backups - Azure Backup | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-support-matrix-iaas)

Your company's Azure subscription contains Azure virtual machines (VMs) that run Windows Server 2016.  
  
One of the VMs is backed up daily by using Azure Backup Instant Restore.  
  
When the VM is infected with data-encrypting ransomware, you decide to recover the VM's files.  
  
Which statement is **TRUE** in this scenario?

options.text: You can only recover the files to the infected VM.
You can recover the files to any VM within the company's subscription.
You can only recover the files to a new VM.
You will not be able to recover the files.

questions.explanation:
Azure Backup file-level recovery for Windows VMs uses the recovery point to mount the backed-up volumes and copy out the needed files. Microsoft Learn states that specific files can be restored to the same or a compatible operating system as the backed-up VM, so recovery is not limited to the original infected VM and does not require creating a new VM. In this scenario, another Windows Server 2016 VM in the same subscription is a compatible target, so the files can be recovered to any such VM.

**Learn more:** [About the Azure Virtual Machine restore process - Azure Backup | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/about-azure-vm-restore) · [Restore VMs by using the Azure portal using Azure Backup - Azure Backup | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-azure-arm-restore-vms)

You have an Azure subscription that contains the storage accounts shown in the following table.

Which storage account can be converted to zone-redundant storage (ZRS) replication?
questions.explanation:
A Standard general-purpose v2 storage account that uses locally redundant storage (LRS) supports conversion to zone-redundant storage (ZRS). An RA-GRS account must first be changed to LRS before a ZRS conversion, and Premium BlobStorage accounts do not support conversion to ZRS.\
\
**Learn more:** [Change how a storage account is replicated - Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/redundancy-migration)

You need to ensure that VM1 can communicate with VM4. The solution must minimize the administrative effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create an NSG and associate the NSG to VM1 and VM4.
Establish peering between VNET1 and VNET3.
Assign VM4 an IP address of 10.0.1.5/24.
Create a user-defined route from VNET1 to VNET3.

questions.explanation: Azure virtual network peering provides direct connectivity between resources in different virtual networks over the Microsoft backbone with minimal configuration. NSGs only control allow/deny traffic and do not create network reachability, a user-defined route requires a valid next-hop path and does not by itself connect separate VNets, and changing VM4 to an address in another network's prefix is not the correct way to enable inter-VNet communication. Therefore, peering VNET1 and VNET3 is the lowest-effort way to enable communication.

questions.question:
You need to ensure that VM1 can communicate with VM4. The solution must minimize the administrative effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: IP1, IP2, IP4, and IP5 only
IP1, IP2, IP3, IP4, and IP5

questions.explanation:
Azure Bastion Basic requires a public IP address that is Standard SKU and statically assigned; Bastion uses a regional IPv4 public IP, not a Global tier address. Among the listed addresses, only IP1 matches all required properties: IPv4, Standard, Regional, and Static. IP2 is Global tier, IP3 and IP4 use Basic SKU, and IP5 is IPv6 and not statically assigned.

**Learn more:** [Manage a public IP address with Azure Bastion - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/configure-public-ip-bastion) · [About Azure Bastion configuration settings - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bastion/configuration-settings)

You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named `contosocloud.onmicrosoft.com`.  
  
Your company has a public DNS zone for `contoso.com`.  
  
You add `contoso.com` as a custom domain name to Azure AD.  
  
You need to ensure that Azure can verify the domain name.  
  
Which type of DNS record should you create?
questions.explanation:
For Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), custom domain ownership is verified by adding a DNS verification record for the domain. Microsoft documents that this verification can use either a TXT record or an MX record. Since the available choices include MX but not TXT, MX is the correct answer. NSEC, PTR, and RRSIG records are not used for Azure AD custom domain verification.\
\
**Learn more:** [Add your custom domain - Microsoft Entra | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/add-custom-domain)

You plan to create new inbound NAT rules that meet the following requirements:  
  
- Provide Remote Desktop access to VM1 from the internet by using port 3389.  
- Provide Remote Desktop access to VM2 from the internet by using port 3389.  
  
What should you create on LB1 before you can create the new inbound NAT rules?
questions.explanation:
An Azure Load Balancer inbound NAT rule forwards traffic from a **frontend IP configuration** and frontend port to a specific backend instance and backend port. Because inbound NAT rules are associated with the load balancer frontend, the required prerequisite resource type is a frontend IP address configuration. A health probe and a load-balancing rule are used for load-balanced traffic, not as prerequisites for NAT rules, and the backend pool is already present on LB1.

**Learn more:** [Inbound NAT rules - Azure Load Balancer | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/inbound-nat-rules) · [Azure Load Balancer components | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/components)

You have an Azure subscription that contains multiple virtual machines in the West US Azure region.  
  
You need to use Traffic Analytics in Azure Network Watcher to monitor virtual machine traffic.  
  
Which two resources should you create? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: a Data Collection Rule (DCR) in Azure Monitor

questions.explanation:
Azure Network Watcher Traffic Analytics analyzes flow logs and requires two core resources: a **storage account** to store the raw flow logs and a **Log Analytics workspace** where Traffic Analytics processes and presents the traffic data. Microsoft Learn documentation for Traffic Analytics and flow log configuration shows that enabling Traffic Analytics includes specifying both a storage account and a Log Analytics workspace; Azure Monitor workbooks, Microsoft Sentinel, and Data Collection Rules are not required to make Traffic Analytics function.

**Learn more:** [Traffic Analytics Overview - Azure Network Watcher | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/traffic-analytics) · [Manage NSG Flow Logs - Azure Network Watcher | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/nsg-flow-logs-manage)

You need to determine which storage account to use for flow logging of IP traffic from VM5. The solution must satisfy the retention requirements.  
  
Which storage account should you identify?
questions.explanation: NSG flow logging for Azure Network Watcher requires a General Purpose v2 (GPv2) storage account located in the same region as the monitored resource (VM5). Retention policies for flow logs are only available with GPv2 accounts. General Purpose v1 storage does not support retention configuration, and Blob storage and File storage accounts are not compatible with flow logging. Storage2 must be the GPv2 account in the appropriate region that satisfies both the compatibility and retention requirements.

questions.question:

Which storage account should you identify?

options.text: Send to a Log Analytics workspace.
Stream to an Azure event hub.

questions.explanation:
Azure Monitor log queries run against data stored in a Log Analytics workspace. For Azure SQL Database diagnostic settings, sending logs to Log Analytics enables Kusto queries and analysis of collected telemetry. A storage account is primarily for archiving logs, and an Event Hub is for streaming logs to other systems rather than querying them directly in Azure Monitor.

**Learn more:** [Diagnostic Settings in Azure Monitor - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-ie/azure/azure-monitor/platform/diagnostic-settings) · [Configure Streaming Export of Metrics and Resource Logs - Azure SQL Database & Azure SQL Managed Instance | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/metrics-diagnostic-telemetry-logging-streaming-export-configure?view=azuresql)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You are creating a new Azure container instance with the following settings:  
  
- Container name: cont1  
- SKU: Standard  
- OS type: Windows  
- Networking type: Public  
- Memory (GiB): 2.5  
- Number of CPU cores: 2  
  
You find that the **Private** setting for **Networking type** is unavailable.  
  
You need to ensure that cont1 can be configured to use private networking.  
  
Which setting should you change?
questions.explanation:
The setting preventing private networking is the operating system type. Azure Container Instances private networking depends on virtual network deployment support, and Windows container instances are the limiting factor here, so changing the OS type from Windows is what enables the private networking option. Memory, CPU core count, SKU, and the current networking selection do not by themselves remove support for private networking. Microsoft Learn documents Azure Container Instances virtual network scenarios and limitations for this capability.

**Learn more:** [Scenarios to use a virtual network - Azure Container Instances](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-virtual-network-concepts) · [Deploy container group to Azure virtual network - Azure Container Instances](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-vnet)

You need to configure an Azure web app named `contoso.azurewebsites.net` to host `www.contoso.com`.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Create A records named www.contoso.com and asuid.contoso.com.
Create a TXT record named asuid that contains the domain verification ID.
Create a CNAME record named asuid that contains the domain verification ID.
Create a TXT record named www.contoso.com that has a value of contoso.azurewebsites.net.

questions.explanation: Azure App Service requires domain ownership verification before binding a custom domain. This is accomplished by creating a TXT record named `asuid` containing a domain verification ID provided by Azure. This verification step must occur before CNAME mapping. Options A and D use incorrect record types or names, and option C incorrectly specifies a CNAME record for verification.

questions.question:
You need to configure an Azure web app named `contoso.azurewebsites.net` to host `www.contoso.com`.  
  
What should you do first?
questions.explanation:
An internal load balancer is appropriate because it distributes traffic across multiple virtual machines by using a private frontend IP inside the virtual network, which is the typical design for internal line-of-business applications accessed over VPN or from on-premises networks. Azure Application Gateway is also valid because it can be deployed with a private frontend IP for internal applications and can load balance requests to backend virtual machines while remaining private to the virtual network. Traffic Manager is not suitable for this requirement because it is DNS-based for internet-facing routing and does not route traffic to private-network endpoints such as internal load balancers.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer components | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/components) · [Configure an application gateway with an internal load balancer (ILB) endpoint](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/configure-application-gateway-with-private-frontend-ip)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains a container group named Group1. Group1 includes two Azure container instances, as shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784205794186-3af4dbp0.png)  
  
You need to ensure that container2 can use CPU resources without adversely affecting container1.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Increase the resource limit of container1 to three CPUs.
Increase the resource limit of container2 to six CPUs.
Remove the resource limit for both containers.
Decrease the resource limit of container2 to two CPUs.

questions.explanation:
In Azure Container Instances, resource requests determine the container group’s allocated CPU capacity. A configured resource limit can allow a container to use CPU above its request, which can reduce CPU available to other containers in the group. Without a resource limit, a container’s maximum usage equals its resource request; therefore, removing both limits caps container1 at 2 CPUs and container2 at 3 CPUs, preventing container2 from consuming CPU needed by container1.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to container groups - Azure Container Instances](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-container-groups)

options.text: From Azure Cost Management, view Cost Analysis

questions.explanation:

You have an Azure virtual machine named VM1 and an Azure key vault named Vault1.  
  
On VM1, you plan to configure Azure Disk Encryption to use a key encryption key (KEK).  
  
You need to prepare Vault1 for Azure Disk Encryption.  
  
Which two actions should you perform on Vault1? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Select Azure Virtual machines for deployment.
Select Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption.

questions.explanation:
To prepare a key vault for Azure Disk Encryption with a key encryption key, you must create a key in the vault to serve as the KEK, and you must enable the "Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption" access policy so the platform can retrieve it during encryption. "Azure Virtual Machines for deployment" is a separate access policy (EnabledForDeployment) used for retrieving certificates during ARM template/VM deployment, and key rotation policies and secrets are not required to enable KEK-based disk encryption.

**Learn more:** [Creating and configuring a key vault for Azure Disk Encryption - Azure Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/disk-encryption-key-vault)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You create an Azure Storage account.  
  
You plan to add 10 blob containers to the storage account.  
  
For one of the containers, you need to use a different key to encrypt data at rest.  
  
What should you do before you create the container?
questions.explanation:
To use a different encryption key for a specific blob container in an Azure Storage account, you must create an **encryption scope** and then assign that scope as the container's default encryption scope when the container is created. Encryption scopes let Azure Storage apply a distinct Microsoft-managed key or customer-managed key at the blob or container level within the same storage account.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage encryption scopes - Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/encryption-scope-manage) · [Encryption scopes for Blob storage - Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/encryption-scope-overview)

questions.question:
Solution: From the **Overview** blade, you move the virtual machine to a different subscription.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: Changing an Azure virtual machine to a different subscription does not move it to another physical host to avoid upcoming maintenance. A subscription move changes the resource’s management scope, whereas host relocation for maintenance requires a maintenance-related action such as redeploying the VM, which places it on a new Azure host.

questions.question:
Solution: On the **Redeploy** blade, you select **Redeploy**.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Redeploying an Azure virtual machine moves it to a new Azure host, which is the appropriate action when the VM must be moved immediately because of host-related maintenance or similar platform issues. Microsoft Learn describes redeploy as shutting down the VM, moving it to a new node, and powering it back on, so this action satisfies the requirement to move VM1 to a different host.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure virtual machines restart operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/virtual-machines/restart-vm) · [Redeploy virtual machine to new Azure node](https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/redeploy-to-new-node-windows)

questions.question:
Solution: From the **Update management** blade, you click **Enable**.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Enabling Update management configures patch and update operations for the guest operating system, but it does not relocate the virtual machine to another physical host. To move an Azure VM immediately to a different host in response to maintenance, the required operation is **redeploy**, which moves the VM to a new Azure node while preserving its configuration and attached resources.\
\
**Learn more:** [Redeploy Windows virtual machines in Azure - Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/redeploy-to-new-node-windows) · [Azure Update Manager Overview | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/overview)

questions.question:
Solution: From the **Overview** blade, you move the virtual machine to another resource group.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: Changing an Azure virtual machine's resource group only changes its resource organization in Azure Resource Manager; it does not relocate the VM to a different physical host. To move a VM immediately to a new host in response to maintenance, the required action is to redeploy the VM, which places it on a new Azure node. Therefore, this solution does not meet the stated goal.

questions.domain: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
questions.question:
Solution: From the resource group pane, move VM1 to a different subscription.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Moving an Azure virtual machine to another subscription does not relocate it to a different physical host. Redeploying the virtual machine moves it to a new Azure host, which is the operation required to address host maintenance.\
\
**Learn more:** [Redeploy Windows virtual machines in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/redeploy-to-new-node-windows) · [Maintenance for virtual machines in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/maintenance-and-updates)

questions.question:
Solution: In the **Redeploy + reapply** blade for VM1, select **Redeploy**.  
  
Does this accomplish the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure VM redeployment shuts down the virtual machine, moves it to a new Azure host/node, and powers it back on while retaining its configuration and associated resources. This moves the VM away from the host affected by maintenance.\
\
**Learn more:** [Redeploy Windows virtual machines in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/redeploy-to-new-node-windows) · [Maintenance for virtual machines in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/maintenance-and-updates)

questions.domain: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
questions.question:
Solution: In the VM1 **Updates** blade, choose **One-time update**.  
  
Does this accomplish the goal?
questions.explanation:
A one-time update installs guest operating-system updates by using Azure Update Manager; it does not redeploy the virtual machine to another physical host. A redeploy operation is required when the VM must run on a new host.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Update Manager operations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/update-manager/workflow-update-manager) · [Scheduled Events for Azure Virtual Machines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/scheduled-events-overview)

Solution: In the VM1 **Updates** blade, choose **One-time update**.  
  
Does this accomplish the goal?
questions.explanation:
An NSG can be associated with a subnet or with a VM's network interface, and each subnet or NIC can have only one associated NSG. The web requirement can be handled with one NSG for Subnet2 and one NSG for Subnet3, because the VMs in each of those subnets need the same inbound rule set. Subnet1 is different because VM1 and VM2 share the subnet, but only VM1 must allow inbound RDP. A single subnet-level NSG cannot permit RDP to VM1 without also permitting it to VM2, so VM1 needs its own NIC-level NSG while the web subnets use their own subnet-level NSGs. That makes the minimum 3 NSGs.

**Learn more:** [Network security groups and application security groups | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/network-application-security-groups) · [Diagnose a virtual machine network traffic filter problem - Azure | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-network/diagnose-network-traffic-filter-problem)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your on-premises network contains a VPN gateway.  
  
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783643047091-1vxiff6d.png)  
  
You need to ensure that all traffic from VM1 to storage1 travels across the Microsoft backbone network.  
  
What should you configure?
questions.explanation:
Azure Storage private endpoints let clients in a virtual network access a storage account through Azure Private Link by using a private IP address in the VNet. Microsoft documents that traffic between virtual network clients and the storage account traverses the virtual network and a private link on the Microsoft backbone network, rather than the public Internet. That is the configuration that satisfies the requirement for VM1-to-storage1 traffic.

**Learn more:** [Use private endpoints for Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-private-endpoints) · [What is a private endpoint? - Azure Private Link](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a Recovery Services vault that you use to test backups. The test backups include two protected virtual machines.  
  
You need to delete the Recovery Services vault.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: From the Recovery Service vault, delete the backup data.
Modify the disaster recovery properties of each virtual machine.
Modify the locks of each virtual machine.
From the Recovery Service vault, stop the backup of each backup item.

questions.explanation:
A Recovery Services vault can't be deleted while it still contains backup-protected items. For protected Azure virtual machines, the required first action is to stop backup/protection for each backup item from the vault, typically using the stop protection and delete data workflow so the backup items and recovery points are removed. Changing VM disaster recovery properties or locks does not satisfy the vault-deletion requirement.

**Learn more:** [Delete a Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Vault - Azure Backup](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-azure-delete-vault) · [Manage recovery points - Azure Backup](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/manage-recovery-points)

From which devices can you use **AzCopy** to copy data to **storage1**?
questions.explanation:
AzCopy v10 is supported on officially maintained versions of Windows, Linux, and macOS. Because Device1 runs Windows 10, Device2 runs Linux, and Device3 runs macOS, each of those devices can run AzCopy and copy data to the Azure Storage account.\

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure container registry named **ContReg1**.  
  
You enable the **Admin user** for **ContReg1**.  
  
Which username can you use to sign in to **ContReg1**?
questions.explanation: When the Azure Container Registry admin account is enabled, Azure creates a single built-in login whose **username is the container registry name** and whose credentials include generated passwords. Therefore, for a registry named **ContReg1**, the valid sign-in username is **ContReg1**.

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You plan to deploy an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster to support an app named App1. On-premises clients will connect to App1 by using the IP address of the pod.  
  
For the AKS cluster, you need to select a network type that will support App1.  
  
What should you choose?
questions.explanation: Azure Container Networking Interface (CNI) is the AKS network model that assigns each pod an IP address from the Azure virtual network, so pod IPs are directly routable on the network and can be reached from connected on-premises environments. Kubenet uses an overlay-style pod address space with NAT and does not make pod IPs directly addressable from on-premises clients. Hybrid Connection endpoints and Azure Private Link are not AKS pod-networking types for this requirement.

Solution: You remove the **BlockAllOther443** inbound security rule.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation: Azure network security group rules are evaluated in priority order, from the lowest number to the highest, and processing stops at the first match. A specific allow rule for source **131.107.100.50** on **TCP port 443** with priority **100** takes precedence over the broader deny rule **BlockAllOther443** at priority **200**. Because that traffic is already matched by the higher-priority allow rule, deleting the deny rule would not be what makes the connection succeed.

questions.question:
Solution: You remove the **BlockAllOther443** inbound security rule.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
An NSG rule that allows traffic from the `AzureLoadBalancer` service tag only affects traffic identified as coming from the Azure Load Balancer, such as load balancer health probes. It does not allow client traffic from `131.107.100.50`. Azure NSG evaluation is first-match-wins in ascending priority order, and the default `AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound` rule already exists at priority `65001`. Adding another AzureLoadBalancer allow rule at priority `150` does not newly permit the required HTTPS connection from the external client source, so it does not resolve the access problem.

**Learn more:** [Network security groups and application security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/network-application-security-groups) · [Troubleshoot NSG misconfigurations that block traffic in Azure Virtual Network](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-troubleshoot-nsg-blocking-traffic)

Solution: You create an inbound security rule that blocks all traffic from the `131.107.100.50` source and has a priority of `64999`.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure network security group rules are processed in priority order, with lower numbers evaluated before higher numbers, and evaluation stops at the first matching rule. The effective rules already include an inbound **Allow** for source `131.107.100.50` on TCP port `443` at priority `100`, so that traffic is already permitted before later rules are checked. Adding a **Deny** rule for that same source at priority `64999` would be lower priority than the existing allow rule and would not enable successful connections. The proposed change therefore does not meet the requirement.

**Learn more:** [Network security groups and application security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/networking/design-guide/network-application-security-groups) · [How Network Security Groups Filter Network Traffic in Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-group-how-it-works)

questions.question:
Solution: You change the priority of the **Allow_131.107.100.50** inbound security rule.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation: In an Azure network security group, rules are evaluated by priority from the lowest number to the highest, and processing stops at the first match. The **Allow_131.107.100.50** rule already has a higher precedence than the broader deny rule for port 443, so traffic from **131.107.100.50** on **TCP 443** would already match the allow rule before the deny rule is considered. Because that allow rule is already ordered correctly, modifying its priority would not fix the connectivity problem.

questions.question:
Solution: You create an inbound security rule that denies all traffic from the `131.107.100.50` source and has a priority of `64999`.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure network security group rules are evaluated in order of priority, from the lowest number to the highest, and processing stops at the first matching rule. An existing inbound rule that allows TCP port 443 from `131.107.100.50` with priority `100` already takes precedence over later rules, including the existing deny on port 443 at priority `200`. Adding another deny rule at priority `64999` would be processed even later and would not enable the required connection; it would only add another lower-priority deny that does not solve the problem. The proposed change therefore does not meet the goal.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure network security groups overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview)

questions.question:
Solution: You create an inbound security rule that allows any traffic from the **AzureLoadBalancer** source and has a priority of **150**.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation: An Azure Load Balancer does not require the application traffic itself to be allowed from the `AzureLoadBalancer` tag. The `AzureLoadBalancer` service tag is primarily used so health probes can reach the VM, and an allow rule for that already exists by default. For client connections to App1 over TCP 443, the NSG must allow the actual client source address. Because the proposed new rule only allows `AzureLoadBalancer` at priority 150, it does not address the failing traffic from `131.107.100.50`, so it does not meet the goal.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains two virtual machines named VM1 and VM2.  
  
You create an Azure load balancer.  
  
You plan to create a load-balancing rule that will balance HTTPS traffic between VM1 and VM2.  
  
Which two additional load balancer resources must you create before you can create the load-balancing rule? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation: Creating a load-balancing rule requires two additional mandatory resources: a backend pool (containing the VMs that will receive traffic, such as VM1 and VM2) and a health probe (determining which backend instances are healthy and eligible to receive traffic). The frontend IP address is created with the load balancer itself. Inbound NAT rules are for one-to-one port mapping rather than load balancing, and a virtual network is infrastructure rather than a load balancer resource component.

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1.  
  
You have 5 TB of data that you need to transfer to Subscription1.  
  
You plan to use an Azure Import/Export job.  
  
What can you use as the destination for the imported data?

options.text: the Azure File Sync Storage Sync Service

questions.explanation:
Azure Import/Export can import data only into Azure Storage targets, specifically Azure Blob storage or Azure Files. Therefore, the valid destination here is Azure File Storage. Services such as Azure Data Factory, Azure File Sync's Storage Sync Service, and Azure SQL Database are not supported import destinations for an Azure Import/Export job.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Import/Export documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/import-export/) · [What is Azure Import/Export service?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/import-export/storage-import-export-service)

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1.  
  
You have 5 TB of data that you need to transfer to Subscription1.  
  
You plan to use an Azure Import/Export job.  
  
What can you use as the destination for the imported data?

options.text: Assign User1 the Contributor role for VNet1.
Assign User1 the Network Contributor role for VNet1.
Assign User1 the User Access Administrator role for VNet1.
Remove User1 from the Security Reader and Reader roles for Subscription1. Assign User1 the Contributor role for Subscription1.

questions.explanation:
Assigning Azure RBAC roles requires the `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` permission at the target scope. The built-in **User Access Administrator** role provides permission to manage user access to Azure resources, including creating role assignments, whereas **Contributor** and **Network Contributor** do not allow granting access. Scoping **User Access Administrator** to **VNet1** gives User1 the ability to assign the **Reader** role for that virtual network without broader unnecessary permissions.

**Learn more:** [Assign Azure roles using the Azure portal - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/role-assignments-portal) · [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783630289028-6tywc9pf.png)  
  
Store1 contains a file share named **data**. **Data** contains 5,000 files.  
  
You need to synchronize the files in the file share named **data** to an on-premises server named **Server1**.  
  
Which three actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Install the Azure File Sync agent on Server1

questions.explanation: Azure File Sync requires three mandatory steps before synchronization is operational: first, install the Azure File Sync agent on the on-premises server to enable Windows Server to sync with Azure file shares; second, register the server with the Storage Sync Service to establish a trust relationship; third, create a sync group that defines the sync topology between the Azure file share (cloud endpoint) and the on-premises server path (server endpoint). Container instances, automation scripts, and network infrastructure are not part of this workflow.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have two Azure subscriptions named Sub1 and Sub2 that are linked to separate Microsoft Entra tenants.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784205609420-kl1z593f.png)  
  
You have the virtual networks listed in the following table.  
  
Which virtual networks can be peered with VNet1?
questions.explanation:
Azure virtual network peering supports virtual networks in the same or different Azure regions through local or global peering. It also supports virtual networks in different subscriptions and Microsoft Entra tenants, provided the required permissions are assigned and the virtual network address spaces do not overlap. Thus, every listed virtual network can be peered with VNet1.

**Learn more:** [Azure Virtual Network peering overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-peering-overview) · [Azure Virtual Network FAQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-faq)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription named Subscription1 that contains a virtual network named VNet1. VNet1 is in a resource group named RG1.  
  
Subscription1 has a user named User1. User1 has the following roles:  
  
- Reader  
- Security Admin  
- Security Reader  
  
You need to ensure that User1 can assign the Reader role for VNet1 to other users.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Remove User1 from the Security Reader role for Subscription1. Assign User1 the Contributor role for RG1.
Assign User1 the Owner role for VNet1.
Assign User1 the Contributor role for VNet1.
Assign User1 the Network Contributor role for VNet1.

questions.explanation:
Assigning an Azure RBAC role requires the `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write` permission at the target scope. The built-in **Owner** role includes the ability to manage all resources **and** assign roles in Azure RBAC, so giving User1 **Owner** on **VNet1** lets User1 grant the **Reader** role for that virtual network. **Contributor** and **Network Contributor** do not allow RBAC role assignment, and the security roles do not provide that permission either.

**Learn more:** [Assign Azure roles using the Azure portal - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/role-assignments-portal) · [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles)

Subscription1 includes a user named User1. User1 has the following roles:  
  
- Reader  
- Security Admin  
- Security Reader  
  
You need to ensure that User1 can assign the Reader role for VNet1 to other users.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Remove User1 from the Security Reader and Reader roles for Subscription1.
Assign User1 the User Access Administrator role for VNet1.
Assign User1 the Network Contributor role for VNet1.
Assign User1 the Network Contributor role for RG1.

questions.explanation: Assigning Azure RBAC roles requires permission to create role assignments at the target scope. The built-in **User Access Administrator** role grants permission to manage user access to Azure resources, including role assignments, while **Reader**, **Security Admin**, **Security Reader**, and **Network Contributor** do not grant RBAC delegation rights. Scoping **User Access Administrator** to **VNet1** allows User1 to assign the **Reader** role for that virtual network without granting broader access.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains the identities shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783632874579-12xoj5ka.png)  
  
User1, Principal1, and Group1 are assigned the Monitoring Reader role.  
  
An action group named AG1 uses the **Email Azure Resource Manager Role** notification type and is configured to email the Monitoring Reader role.  
  
You create an alert rule named Alert1 that uses AG1.  
  
You need to identify who will receive an email notification when Alert1 is triggered.  
  
Who should you identify?
questions.explanation:
For an Azure Monitor action group that uses **Email Azure Resource Manager Role**, Azure sends notifications only to Microsoft Entra ID **user** members of the selected Azure RBAC role. Directly assigned managed identities do not receive email notifications, and managed identities inside a role-assigned group do not receive them either. Because the Monitoring Reader role is assigned to **User1** directly and to **Group1**, and **User2** is the user member of Group1, the email goes to **User1 and User2** only.

**Learn more:** [Create and manage action groups in Azure Monitor - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/action-groups)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains a virtual machine named VM1. VM1 hosts a line-of-business application that is available 24 hours a day. VM1 has one network interface and one managed disk. VM1 uses the D4s v3 size.  
  
You plan to make the following changes to VM1:  
  
- Change the size to D8s v3.  
- Add a 500-GB managed disk.  
- Add the Puppet Agent extension.  
- Enable Desired State Configuration Management.  
  
Which change will cause downtime for VM1?

options.text: Change the size to D8s v3

questions.explanation:
Resizing an Azure virtual machine causes the VM to restart if it is running, and some resize operations also require the VM to be deallocated first. That restart is downtime. Adding a managed data disk and installing VM extensions are performed through Azure's disk and guest agent mechanisms and do not inherently require the VM to be stopped. Enabling Desired State Configuration management uses the DSC extension asynchronously to onboard the VM rather than requiring a platform shutdown.

**Learn more:** [Resize a virtual machine - Azure Virtual Machines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/sizes/resize-vm) · [Enable Azure Automation State Configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/automation/automation-dsc-onboarding)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have five Azure virtual machines that run Windows Server 2016. The virtual machines are configured as web servers.  
  
You have an Azure load balancer named LB1 that provides load-balancing services for the virtual machines.  
  
You need to ensure that visitors are serviced by the same web server for each request.  
  
What should you configure?

options.text: Floating IP (direct server return) to Disabled

questions.explanation:
Azure Load Balancer achieves this requirement by enabling session persistence, also called source IP affinity. Setting **Session persistence** to **Client IP** causes successive requests from the same client IP address to be sent to the same backend virtual machine, which provides the needed server stickiness for the web servers. Floating IP, protocol selection, and idle timeout do not control backend affinity.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer distribution modes | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/distribution-mode-concepts) · [Azure Load Balancer portal settings | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/manage)

For an Azure Resource Manager deployment that creates multiple resources in a resource group, the exact template used is available from that resource group's **Deployments** history. Microsoft Learn states that to export the template used after deployment, you select the resource group, open **Deployments**, choose the deployment, and then select **Template**. That makes the resource group blade the correct place to start, which here is **RG1**.

**Learn more:** [Export template in Azure portal - Azure Resource Manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/export-template-portal) · [Deploy resources with ARM templates and Azure portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-portal)

What should you configure for container1?
questions.explanation:
DNS name label scope reuse in Azure Container Instances is a setting for the container group's public DNS name label and FQDN. Microsoft Learn documents that this option is configured on the **Networking** tab for an ACI deployment that uses a public endpoint. Because the setting applies to the public DNS label, container1 must use the public networking type rather than private networking in a VNet. A subnet and a confidential SKU do not enable this capability.

You create a route table named RT1 in the East US Azure region.  
  
Which resources can you associate with RT1?
questions.explanation:
An Azure route table can be associated with one or more subnets in virtual networks in the same subscription and Azure region. It cannot be associated directly with a virtual network or a network interface. Subnet1 is in East US, the same region as RT1.\
\
**Learn more:** [Create, change, or delete an Azure route table](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/manage-route-table)

options.text: From VM1, install the Windows Server Backup feature.
From VM2, install the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Agent.
From VM1, install the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services Agent.
From VM2, install the Windows Server Backup feature.

questions.explanation:
File and folder backup to an Azure Recovery Services vault uses the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) agent. When recovering that data to a different server, Azure Backup supports an alternate server or alternate machine restore through the MARS agent installed on the destination machine. Windows Server Backup is relevant for applying restored System State, not for restoring a backed-up folder to another VM.

**Learn more:** [About the MARS Agent - Azure Backup | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-azure-about-mars) · [Restore files to Windows Server using the MARS Agent - Azure Backup | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/backup/backup-azure-restore-windows-server)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to make sure that VM1 can communicate with VM4 while minimizing administrative effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a user-defined route from VNET1 to VNET3.
Create an NSG and associate the NSG to VM1 and VM4.
Assign VM4 an IP address of 10.0.1.5/24.
Establish peering between VNET1 and VNET3.

questions.explanation:
Azure virtual network peering is the simplest built-in way to enable direct private connectivity between resources in two virtual networks. It allows VMs in different VNets to communicate over the Azure backbone without requiring gateways, custom routes to create the connection, or IP reconfiguration. NSGs only permit or deny traffic, and user-defined routes do not by themselves provide reachability between separate VNets. Microsoft Learn documents VNet peering as enabling resources in different VNets to communicate with each other privately.

**Learn more:** [What is virtual network peering?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-network-peering-overview) · [Azure virtual network traffic routing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-udr-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You need to receive an email alert when a resource lock is removed from any resource in the subscription.  
  
What should you use to create an activity log alert in Azure Monitor?

options.text: a resource, a condition, and an action group
a resource, a condition, and a Microsoft 365 group
a Log Analytics workspace, a resource, and an action group
a data collection endpoint, an application security group, and a resource group

questions.explanation:
Azure Monitor activity log alerts are created by selecting the alert scope as the target resource or subscription, defining the Activity Log condition that matches the administrative event such as deleting a lock, and attaching an action group that sends the email notification. Microsoft Learn documents activity log alert creation around scope, condition, and actions via an action group; a Log Analytics workspace or data collection endpoint is not required for this alert type.

**Learn more:** [Create an activity log, service health, or resource health alert rule - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-create-activity-log-alert-rule) · [az monitor activity-log alert | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/monitor/activity-log/alert?view=azure-cli-latest)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster named AKS1.  
  
You need to configure cluster autoscaler for AKS1.  
  
Which two tools should you use? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
**NOTE:** Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation:
In AKS, cluster autoscaler is an Azure-managed configuration for the cluster or node pool, so you configure it through AKS management tools such as Azure CLI or the Azure portal. Microsoft Learn shows enabling and updating cluster autoscaler with `az aks update` using `--enable-cluster-autoscaler`, `--min-count`, and `--max-count`. `kubectl` does not configure this Azure resource setting, `Set-AzVm` applies to standalone virtual machines rather than AKS, and `Set-AzAks` is not the valid AKS PowerShell cmdlet name.

**Learn more:** [az aks | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/aks?view=azure-cli-latest) · [Use the cluster autoscaler in Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/cluster-autoscaler)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure Storage account that contains 5,000 blobs that are accessed by multiple users.  
  
You need to make sure the users can view only certain blobs based on blob index tags.  
  
What should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation:
Azure Blob Storage supports Azure attribute-based access control (ABAC), which extends Azure RBAC with **role assignment conditions**. Those conditions can restrict blob access based on blob index tag key/value pairs, allowing users to read only blobs whose tags match the defined rule. A stored access policy or SAS delegates access but does not provide the same RBAC tag-based authorization model for enforcing per-user visibility rules across blobs, and JIT VM access is unrelated to blob access control.

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Add a role assignment condition to restrict access to blobs using the Azure portal](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-auth-abac-portal) · [Authorize access to Azure Blob Storage using Azure role assignment conditions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-auth-abac)

You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Storage account.  
  
You plan to create an Azure container instance named **container1** that will use a Docker image named **Image1**. **Image1** contains a Microsoft SQL Server instance that requires persistent storage.  
  
You need to configure a storage service for **container1**.  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
Azure Container Instances provides persistent volume support by mounting an Azure Files share into the container. That gives a SQL Server container durable filesystem storage that remains available across container restarts. Azure Blob storage, Queue storage, and Table storage are not the appropriate persistent mounted storage service for this container volume requirement.

**Learn more:** [Mount an Azure file share in Azure Container Instances](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-volume-azure-files) · [Azure Container Instances volumes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-instances/container-instances-container-groups#volumes)

questions.domain: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription that contains a web app named **webapp1**.  
  
You need to add a custom domain named **www.contoso.com** to **webapp1**.  
  
What should you do first?
questions.explanation: Adding a custom hostname to an Azure App Service app begins with DNS configuration for that hostname so Azure can verify ownership and route traffic correctly. For a subdomain such as **www.contoso.com**, this is typically done by creating a **CNAME** record that maps the name to the app's default domain name. TLS certificates are added afterward if HTTPS is required; connection strings and stopping the app are unrelated.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You create the following Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template to create a resource group and deploy an Azure Storage account to that resource group.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783638181040-h38tsodw.jpg)  
  
Which cmdlet should you run to deploy the template?
questions.explanation:
Because the template creates a **resource group** and then performs a nested deployment into that resource group, the deployment must start at **subscription scope**. Microsoft Learn specifies that `New-AzDeployment` creates a deployment at the current subscription scope, which is the correct scope for templates that create resource groups. `New-AzResourceGroupDeployment` is for deployments to an **existing** resource group, `New-AzTenantDeployment` is for tenant-scope deployments, and `New-AzResource` is for creating resources without using an ARM template.

**Learn more:** [New-AzDeployment (Az.Resources)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.resources/new-azdeployment) · [New-AzResourceGroupDeployment (Az.Resources)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.resources/new-azresourcegroupdeployment)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your on-premises network includes a VPN gateway.  
  
You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783646430566-zoxam746.png)  
  
You need to make sure that all traffic from VM1 to storage1 travels over the Microsoft backbone network.  
  
What should you configure?
questions.explanation: Azure service endpoints are used to keep traffic from a virtual network to supported Azure services, such as Azure Storage, on the Microsoft backbone network. In this scenario, VM1 is connected to Vnet1 and that virtual network has forced tunneling enabled, so configuring a service endpoint for Azure Storage on the VM1 subnet ensures access to storage1 uses the Azure backbone rather than being sent through the site-to-site VPN path. NSGs only control allow/deny rules, Azure Firewall is not the required mechanism for private optimized routing to the storage account, and Azure AD Application Proxy is for publishing applications, not Storage connectivity.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You create an Azure VM named VM1 that runs Windows Server 2019.  
  
VM1 is configured as shown in the exhibit. (Click the Exhibit tab.)  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783631027671-ssf36jwl.jpg)  
  
You need to enable Desired State Configuration for VM1.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Configure a DNS name for VM1.

questions.explanation:
Desired State Configuration on an Azure virtual machine is enabled by installing and using the DSC extension or onboarding the VM to Azure Automation State Configuration, and Azure VM extensions can be installed only when the VM is running. Because VM1 is currently stopped (deallocated), the required first step is to start the virtual machine before enabling DSC.

**Learn more:** [Use the Azure Desired State Configuration extension for Windows](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/dsc-windows) · [Virtual machine extensions and features for Windows](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/features-windows)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are planning to deploy three Azure virtual machines named VM1, VM2, and VM3. The virtual machines will host a web app named App1.  
  
You need to make sure that at least two virtual machines remain available if a single Azure datacenter becomes unavailable.  
  
What should you deploy?

options.text: all three virtual machines in a single Availability Zone
all virtual machines in a single Availability Set
each virtual machine in a separate Availability Zone
each virtual machine in a separate Availability Set

questions.explanation:
Availability Zones provide datacenter-level fault isolation because they are physically separate locations within an Azure region. Placing VM1, VM2, and VM3 in separate Availability Zones ensures that if one datacenter/zone becomes unavailable, the other two VMs can continue running. Availability Sets are designed to protect against hardware and maintenance failures within a datacenter, not the loss of an entire datacenter.

**Learn more:** [What are Azure availability zones?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-ie/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview) · [Availability sets overview - Azure Virtual Machines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/availability-set-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have five Azure virtual machines that run Windows Server 2016. The virtual machines are configured as web servers.  
  
You have an Azure load balancer named **LB1** that provides load-balancing services for the virtual machines.  
  
You need to ensure that visitors are serviced by the same web server for each request.  
  
What should you configure?

options.text: Floating IP (direct server return) to Disabled
Floating IP (direct server return) to Enabled

questions.explanation:
Azure Load Balancer provides client affinity through **session persistence**. Setting **Session persistence to Client IP** uses source IP affinity so successive requests from the same client IP address are handled by the same backend virtual machine. **Floating IP** relates to direct server return behavior, and a **health probe** is only used to detect whether backend instances are available, not to keep a client on the same server.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer distribution modes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/distribution-mode-concepts) · [Configure Azure Load Balancer distribution mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/load-balancer-distribution-mode)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure AD tenant that contains the groups shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783645821290-3qpnkkjn.png)  
  
You purchase Azure Active Directory Premium P2 licenses.  
  
To which groups can you assign a license?
questions.explanation:
Group-based licensing in Microsoft Entra ID supports assigning licenses to security groups, including mail-enabled security groups, and to Microsoft 365 groups that are security-enabled. A Microsoft 365 group that is not security-enabled can't be used for license assignment. Therefore, the eligible groups are Group1, Group2, and Group3.

**Learn more:** [Assign Microsoft 365 licenses to user accounts - Microsoft 365 Enterprise | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/enterprise/assign-licenses-to-user-accounts?view=o365-worldwide) · [group: assignLicense - Microsoft Graph v1.0 | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/graph/api/group-assignlicense?view=graph-rest-1.0)

options.text: Modify the Public network access settings.

questions.explanation:
Azure Storage public network access can be configured as enabled from selected networks, which allows specific virtual networks and public IP address ranges. This supports selected Azure networks and a home office public IP address with storage-account network rules. Private endpoints are used when public network access is disabled and require additional private networking configuration; Internet routing does not restrict access, and IAM does not configure network access.

**Learn more:** [Set the default public network access rule for an Azure Storage account](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-network-security-set-default-access) · [Azure Storage firewall rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-network-security)

You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant named `contoso.onmicrosoft.com`.  
  
The **User administrator** role is assigned to a user named **Admin1**.  
  
An external partner has a Microsoft account that uses the `[email protected]` sign-in.  
  
Admin1 tries to invite the external partner to sign in to the Azure AD tenant and receives the following error message:  
  
`Unable to invite user [email protected] "` Generic authorization exception.`  
  
You need to ensure that Admin1 can invite the external partner to sign in to the Azure AD tenant.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: From the Users settings blade, modify the External collaboration settings.
From the Custom domain names blade, add a custom domain.
From the Organizational relationships blade, add an identity provider.
From the Roles and administrators blade, assign the Security administrator role to Admin1.

questions.explanation: Guest invitations in Azure AD / Microsoft Entra ID are controlled by B2B external collaboration settings, including who is allowed to invite guest users. A User Administrator can invite guests only when the tenant’s external collaboration configuration permits it. A personal Microsoft account does not require adding a custom domain or a separate identity provider for standard B2B collaboration, and assigning Security Administrator does not address guest invitation restrictions. The required change is to modify the External collaboration settings in Users settings so Admin1 is permitted to send the invitation.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a registered DNS domain named `contoso.com`.  
  
You create a public Azure DNS zone named `contoso.com`.  
  
You need to ensure that records created in the `contoso.com` zone are resolvable from the internet.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Modify the SOA record in the DNS domain registrar.
Create the SOA record in contoso.com.
Modify the NS records in the DNS domain registrar.

questions.explanation:
A public Azure DNS zone becomes publicly resolvable only after the domain is delegated to the Azure DNS name servers assigned to that zone. That delegation is done at the domain registrar by updating the domain’s NS records in the parent zone. The SOA and zone-apex NS records are automatically created in Azure DNS, so the needed action is to change the registrar’s NS records to the Azure-provided name servers.

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Host your domain in Azure DNS](https://learn.microsoft.com/mt-mt/azure/dns/dns-delegate-domain-azure-dns) · [FAQ - Azure DNS](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/dns/dns-faq)

You have five Azure virtual machines that run Windows Server 2016. The virtual machines are configured as web servers.  
  
You have an Azure load balancer named LB1 that provides load-balancing services for the virtual machines.  
  
You need to ensure that visitors are served by the same web server for each request.  
  
What should you configure?

options.text: Floating IP (direct server return) to Enabled
Floating IP (direct server return) to Disabled
Session persistence to Client IP and Protocol

questions.explanation:
Azure Load Balancer keeps a client mapped to the same backend by using **session persistence** (source IP affinity). The **Client IP and Protocol** distribution mode uses the client source IP plus protocol to maintain affinity so repeated requests from the same visitor continue to reach the same web server. **Floating IP** is for direct server return scenarios, and a **health probe** only monitors instance health rather than preserving client-to-server affinity.

**Learn more:** [Azure Load Balancer distribution modes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/distribution-mode-concepts) · [Azure Load Balancer portal settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/load-balancer/manage)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have 15 Azure subscriptions.  
  
You have an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant that contains a security group named Group1.  
  
You plan to purchase an additional Azure subscription.  
  
You need to ensure that Group1 can manage role assignments for the existing subscriptions and the planned subscriptions. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Use the principle of least privilege.  
- Minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Assign Group1 the Owner role for the root management group.
Assign Group1 the User Access Administrator role for the root management group.
Create a new management group and assign Group1 the User Access Administrator role for the group.
Create a new management group and assign Group1 the Owner role for the group.

questions.explanation:
To let a group manage Azure RBAC role assignments without granting full resource-management permissions, assign the **User Access Administrator** role rather than **Owner**. Assigning that role at the **root management group** scopes the permission at the highest level, so it is inherited by all existing subscriptions and by subscriptions added later in the tenant. That satisfies least privilege and avoids per-subscription administration.

**Learn more:** [Azure built-in roles - Azure RBAC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles) · [Organize your resources with management groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/governance/management-groups/overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure virtual machine named VM1 that runs Windows Server 2019. The VM was deployed by using the default drive settings.  
  
You sign in to VM1 as a user named User1 and perform the following actions:  
  
- Create files on drive C.  
- Create files on drive D.  
- Modify the screen saver timeout.  
- Change the desktop background.  
  
You plan to redeploy VM1.  
  
Which change will be lost after you redeploy VM1?

options.text: the new files on drive D
the new files on drive C

questions.explanation:
Redeploying an Azure VM moves it to a new host but keeps the OS and data disks. With the default Windows Azure VM layout, drive D is the temporary disk, and Microsoft states that data saved on the temporary disk is lost after a redeploy. Files on drive C and user settings such as the screen saver timeout and desktop background are stored on the persistent OS disk, so they are retained.

**Learn more:** [Redeploy Windows virtual machines in Azure - Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/virtual-machines/windows/redeploy-to-new-node-windows) · [Make the D: drive of a VM a data disk - Azure Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/change-drive-letter)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains a storage account named `storage1`. The `storage1` account contains a container named `container1`.  
  
You need to configure access to `container1`. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Only allow read access.  
- Allow both HTTP and HTTPS protocols.  
- Apply access permissions to all the content in the container.  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
A shared access signature (SAS) can be scoped to a blob container, limited to **read** permission, and configured to allow **HTTPS or HTTP/HTTPS**. When issued at the container level, the SAS applies to resources in that container. A stored access policy alone does not grant access by itself; it only defines constraints for a SAS. Access keys provide broad account access rather than read-only delegated access, and Azure CDN does not configure blob container authorization.

**Learn more:** [Grant limited access to Azure Storage resources using shared access signatures (SAS)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview) · [Create a service SAS for a container or blob with .NET](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/sas-service-create-dotnet)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an on-premises server that contains a folder named `D:\Folder1`.  
  
You need to copy the contents of `D:\Folder1` to the public container in an Azure Storage account named `contosodata`.  
  
Which command should you run?

options.text: az storage blob copy start-batch D:\Folder1 https://contosodata.blob.core.windows.net/public

questions.explanation:
AzCopy is the correct utility for uploading data from a local folder to Azure Blob Storage. Microsoft Learn shows that copying an entire local directory to a blob container uses `azcopy copy <local-directory> <container-URL> --recursive=true`. That is exactly the operation needed to copy the contents of `D:\Folder1` into the `public` container. The Azure CLI `az storage blob copy start-batch` command is for server-side blob-to-blob copy operations from Azure storage sources, not for uploading files from a local disk path.

**Learn more:** [azcopy copy - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-ref-azcopy-copy) · [az storage blob copy - Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/storage/blob/copy?view=azure-cli-latest)

You have three offices and an Azure subscription that contains an Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) tenant.  
  
You need to delegate user management permissions to a local administrator in each office.  
  
What should you use?

options.text: access packages in Azure AD entitlement management

questions.explanation:
Administrative units let you segment Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) users, groups, and devices into scoped containers and then assign directory roles within that limited scope. This is the built-in way to delegate user administration to separate office-level administrators without granting tenant-wide Azure AD permissions. Azure AD roles alone are generally tenant-wide, Azure roles apply to Azure resources rather than directory users, and access packages are for entitlement management rather than delegated user administration.

**Learn more:** [Administrative units in Microsoft Entra ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-ie/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/administrative-units) · [Microsoft Entra RBAC documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has two on-premises servers named **SRV01** and **SRV02**. Developers created an application that runs on **SRV01**. The application calls a service on **SRV02** by using its IP address.  
  
You plan to migrate the application to **Azure virtual machines (VMs)**. You have configured **two VMs on a single subnet** in an **Azure virtual network**.  
  
You need to configure the two VMs with **static internal IP addresses**.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Modify the VM properties in the Azure Management Portal.
Modify the IP properties in Windows Network and Sharing Center.

questions.explanation:
Static internal addresses for Azure VMs must be assigned in Azure on the network interface/IP configuration, not by manually setting the guest operating system’s network settings. Microsoft Learn states that a VM’s private IP can be changed to **Static** in Azure and warns against statically assigning the Azure VM private IP from within the operating system. Of the available choices, the cmdlet that directly performs this function in the classic Azure model is **Set-AzureStaticVNetIP**.

**Learn more:** [Create a VM with a static private IP address using the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, or Azure CLI](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/virtual-networks-static-private-ip) · [Configure IP addresses for an Azure network interface](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/virtual-network-network-interface-addresses)
